#7832. What Makes a Lucky Dog? | Heroes of the Pet World

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â

Mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

Different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

That Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â

It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â

Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

Three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â

Some dogs find their people quickly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

At Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

Anyone else been ogling Catherine's Thanksgiving decor on Instagram?

Anyone else already thinking about their holiday tablescapes? Because Catherine Zeta-Jones has just given us all the Thanksgiving inspiration we could ever need.

The actor recently shared a glimpse of her and Michael Douglas's Thanksgiving decor, and it's the kind of rustic autumnal display that makes you want to invite everyone over for dinner; think warm orange foliage, miniature pumpkins, natural branches and a gorgeous leafy garland.

It's the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, and you don't need a celebrity-sized decorating budget to recreate the look. In fact, I'd argue that some of the prettiest ingredients might already be growing in your backyard.

Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of those stars attached to countless big projects, from Wednesday to Chicago to America's Sweethearts. Still, though, she remains wonderfully down-to-earth... and even takes the time to make her own fall decor, too!

'A little DIY in anticipation of Thanksgiving,' she captioned a photo of her table on Instagram. 'I love this up coming holiday, my kids are home from college and I can’t wait!!!'

A post shared by Catherine Zeta-Jones (@catherinezetajones)

Keen to give it a go for yourself? Well, it's easy enough; all you really need to focus on is bringing the beauty of your autumnal garden indoors.

First things first, head outside and gather a selection of autumn leaves in warm shades of orange, red, bronze and gold. Maple and oak leaves are particularly lovely, but don't overlook interesting branches and seasonal greenery, either.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and try using a mixture of different leaf shapes and sizes because it gives the arrangement a more natural, gathered-from-the-garden feel. Then, you can lay the foliage directly along the middle of the table, creating a loose runner that you can build the rest of your decorations around.

Something like the Oasis Forage Floral Create Kit on Amazon could help with this.

This clever little foraging kit has everything you need to get started on crafting your own fall decorations.

Whatever you do, just make sure anything you collect is clean and free from pests. And if you're gathering from outside your garden, always check that you're allowed to collect it.

You can't have a Thanksgiving centerpiece without pumpkins, can you? And Catherine Zeta-Jones's rustic look is a lovely reminder that you don't need enormous pumpkins to make an impact.

I'd choose a mixture of orange, cream and green varieties, placing them at intervals along the foliage. Try grouping a few together rather than spacing everything out too evenly. That slightly imperfect arrangement is what makes the whole thing feel so charming.

If you've grown your own ornamental gourds, even better! They're a wonderful way to give your Thanksgiving decorations a personal touch.

Now for my favorite part: the finishing touches! Honestly, a few interesting branches, seedheads or pinecones will add height and texture to the arrangement, and I particularly love the idea of incorporating dried ornamental grasses, which bring movement and a lovely natural softness to the display.

Then, make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and add small votive candles or LED tealights between the pumpkins and foliage. The warm glow will make the whole table feel wonderfully inviting once the evening draws in.

What I love about Catherine Zeta Jones's rustic decorations is that they remind us how much beauty there is to be found in the changing seasons!

You don't need elaborate floral arrangements or expensive accessories to make a Thanksgiving table feel specia; all it takes is a handful of colorful leaves, a few little pumpkins and some carefully chosen garden finds . Now if you'll excuse me, I think I'll be heading out to the backyard with a basket before all those beautiful fall leaves disappear!

#7830. Wild Bleeding Heart: A Hardworking and Adaptable Beauty

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Here, Melissa Starkey shares about wild bleeding heart, one of her favorite underappreciated native plants to grow.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

This plant is extremely close to my heart because I remember seeing it growing wild in Pennsylvania when I was a child. A great alternative to nonnative common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis and cvs., Zones 3–9), it produces its best flush of heart-shaped flowers in spring but keeps blooming through the entire growing season, even as late as November here at Mt. Cuba Center. Wild bleeding heart also has fernlike foliage, which has a kind of blush tinge.

But all its aesthetic qualities aside, wild bleeding heart is incredibly hardworking and adaptable. It can grow in partial shade and makes an excellent woodland plant. This plant also does quite well out in the sun; it grows naturally on rocky, sunny outcrops. I have seen it growing right out of rocks in the wild. While it does adapt well, its unique flowers require larger pollinators, like bumblebees, that are strong enough to force themselves through its tight petals.

Wild bleeding heart is a bit smaller than common bleeding heart, but it does not go dormant like its nonnative relatives, giving you three seasons of interest. If pink flowers aren’t to your taste, there is a white cultivar available called ‘Alba’ (D. eximia ‘Alba’, Zones 3–9).

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.

#7829. Let’s Be SMART – Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, currently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs.  I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future.  We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

#7827. Plant These 8 Hardy Vegetables in November – They’re Easy to Grow for Fresh Winter and Spring Harvests

Think your vegetable garden is finished for the year? Not so fast. Some crops relish cooler temperatures and can shrug off a little frost.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn’t necessarily mark the end of the vegetable growing season. While warm-season crops are definitely done for the year, you may still be able to sow and grow some of your cold-hardy favorites.

Knowing how and when to plant a vegetable garden so late in the season depends on your USDA hardiness zone, climate, and local weather. If you have milder winters, you can likely sow seeds directly in outdoor beds. In colder climates, you’ll need to provide some protection against frost and snow.

Here, I offer pro tips on late veggie growing, along with eight vegetables you may be able to start now for a winter or spring harvest. If you’re unsure about whether or not you can grow any of these in November, contact your extension office for more location-specific guidance.

Planting veggies now takes more effort than simply sowing seeds. Beyond knowing your climate and hardiness zone, you need to pay attention to the weather. For example, avoid seeding when the soil is frozen or soggy.

Prepare the soil by clearing out weeds, raking out any stones or remaining summer plant debris, and mixing in fresh compost. Seed planting depth and spacing depend on the crop you are sowing, so do check the seed packet information.

Manage your expectations for this project. Less sunlight and colder temperatures mean germination and growth will be slow. Be patient.

Although these veggies are either cold-tolerant or good at overwintering, they still will not tolerate very cold weather. If you have cold winters, you’ll need to protect your efforts. An old milk jug can give seeds some protection and act as a mini greenhouse for a few seeds. If you want to start more seeds, use a cold frame, like the Giantex wooden cold frame, which has a flip top for easy access.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As plants develop, row covers will protect winter veggies from frost, snow, harsh winds, and flying pests. This Plant Covers Freeze Protection Kit on Amazon includes hoops, clips, and a roll of frost blanket.

Apply straw, shredded leaves, or other loose, organic mulch over and around new crops or overwintering veggies. Just take care not to drown delicate seedlings in mulch.

Take care with watering, as letting soil get soggy is easy to do in winter. Check the soil before watering plants.

These are some of our favorite vegetables that many gardeners can start in November, including those that could be ready in winter and others that you’ll harvest in spring or summer.

Garlic is an example of a crop that will overwinter and provide you with a harvest next summer. As long as your soil is workable and not waterlogged, garlic is a dependable crop for planting now. Plant individual garlic cloves with the pointy ends up. Use mulch to protect the cloves from winter freezes. If successful, your cloves will grow roots over winter, foliage in spring, and bulbs in the summer.

You can plant garlic from the grocery store, though it’s usually a softneck variety grown in milder climates and may struggle in colder regions. Hardneck garlic is often a better choice for those areas. Botanical Interests offers an organic garlic flavor sampler bundle featuring two hardneck varieties and elephant garlic.

Shallots can also be overwintered and will reward you with a harvest in late spring or early summer. Plant shallot sets or individual shallot bulbs with the pointy ends up, just slightly above the soil surface. French Red Shallots from Burpee are a delicious culinary variety worth trying.

You should mulch lightly to protect shallots in colder climates. However, fall planting is best suited to milder regions, and if you have very cold winters, the planting window may already have passed. Check with your local extension office for exact dates.

Spinach is remarkably cold-hardy. The seeds will be slow to germinate in the cold, though. This Sow Right Seeds Spinach Seed Collection contains three tasty varieties. Unless you have very mild winters, use cold frames or other protections. Once spinach plants get established, they should produce leaves you can pick throughout the winter. Harvest from the outside edge of the plants, leaving the center intact.

Kale is another very cold-hardy vegetable that many gardeners can grow now for winter harvests. It’s also hard to grow from seed in the cold, so unless you have mild weather in November, consider using transplants, like these Bonnie Plants Lacinato Kale Plants from Lowe's. Use cold frames or row covers as needed, especially during hard freezes. For warmer zones, Burpee sells a four-variety kale blend.

Arugula is a mildly cold-tolerant green that is best for growing in November in milder climates. If conditions are right, it will germinate and grow rapidly, giving you a winter harvest. If you want to grow arugula in colder regions, use frames or a greenhouse and be prepared for growth to be slower. You can pick up a pack of arugula seeds for less than $5 from Sow Right Seeds.

Like arugula, radishes grow rapidly, so if the weather and soil conditions are right, you can start plants now and get a quick winter harvest. Burpee's Cooks Custom Blend Radish Seeds Collection contains red, pink, purple, and white radishes. For the best results, the soil should be workable, and November temperatures should be cool or mild. For colder areas, plant the most cold-tolerant varieties and use cold frames.

Plant carrots now for a sweet treat in early spring. Carrots generally overwinter well, but choose the more cold-tolerant varieties for the best results. Scarlet Nantes, included in this Gardeners Basics 5-Variety Pack on Amazon, can be harvested through winter with protection. It’s also important to make sure the soil is loose and free of stones, so the roots can grow deep. Use a generous layer of mulch to keep the soil warmer over winter.

Peas can also generally be overwintered for a spring harvest. Peas grow best in cooler weather, but they still need some warmth to establish. Alaska peas, available from Eden Brothers, tolerate chilly conditions, but if your November is very cold, it might be too late. In milder growing regions, this can be a good time to start peas. Be sure to plant your peas near a trellis or other vertical structure so the plants can climb in spring.

November doesn’t have to mean the end of growing veggies for the year. Depending on your region and local weather, you may be able to grow or overwinter some or all of these cold-tolerant vegetables. Choose the plants most suited to your conditions and be patient. Colder weather means slower growth.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

So how do you entice picky eaters to keep chowing down without resorting to kitty junk food that wonât serve their health in the long run? We think Made by Nacho has the answer.

There are a number of reasons cats tend to be picky when it comes to mealtime. Depending on your feline, you may be dealing with one or all of these difficult instincts and sensitivities.

To start, cats have a very sensitive sense of smell. Even quality food can be turned down if the aroma is too unfamiliar. Cats are also very finicky about textures. They tend to develop very specific preferences about how foods should feel in their mouth. This makes it both hard to introduce new foods and to keep your cat from getting bored with the very specific foods they like.

Many cats exhibit neophobiaâa fear of new things. This doesnât just apply to new people, places, and toys, either. Cats evolved to be naturally wary of new food items and prey. This is likely because their ancestors lived in the desert where many little creatures are deadlier than their size might indicate. While modern cat food isnât likely to be venomous, your cat's instincts still tell them to beware anything they havenât eaten before.

Itâs the combination of a desire for the familiar and a tendency to get bored of the too familiar that makes picky cats so hard to feed. They want enough options that fall within a very specific range of flavors, textures, and aromas to keep them both interested and comfortable.

This can make adding moisture to their diets challenging, too, especially for cats who prefer dry food over wet. Luckily, simple additions like savory bone broth can help cat parents incorporate more moisture without introducing an entirely unfamiliar meal.

#7825. ‘Fireworks’ Goldenrod: A Pollinator Favorite with Bold Yellow Blooms

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Learn more about ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod, one of Melissa Starkey’s favorite underappreciated native plants.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

We’re moving into fall for this next pick. Goldenrods are amazing plants in general, even though they get a bad rap. People sometimes associate them with allergies, but they are confusing goldenrod with ragweed (Ambrosia spp.). Not all goldenrods are too aggressive. They are host plants for over 120 different moth and butterfly caterpillars, and the seeds feed birds and other animals.

If I had to pick just one to highlight, ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod would be my gateway plant to goldenrods. Anyone can use it in their garden, including in formal settings and in containers. ‘Fireworks’ is an appropriate name for this cultivar, as spires of bright yellow flowers explode in early to mid-autumn. It has a compact, clumping habit. This goldenrod can spread a little bit in moist soil, but it is not difficult to control, and it will stay put if you site it in a drier area. It likes full sun, but I have it in partial shade and it still looks lovely.

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.

#7824. 8 Easy Landscape Designer Tricks to Transition Your Garden From Fall into Winter

A few thoughtful changes will keep your garden landscape looking effortlessly stylish through the cooler seasons.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While you might be thinking that the gardening season is drawing to a close this month, there's plenty to look forward to, especially if make a few simple switches to help your yard transition from fall into winter. As the year segues into the cooler months, it's time to enjoy colorful stems, textural bark, sculptural seedheads and shrubs bejewelled with bright berries, and relish the quiet beauty of this season.

Check through our landscape designer tricks to take a fall yard into winter, and add one or two to your outside space now. An injection of structural evergreens, naturalistic ornamental grasses, a tree with fiery foliage or colorful autumn bulbs can make a huge difference at this time of year now the late-season flower show is coming to an end.

Consider, too, how to make your fall garden user-friendly so you feel inspired to spend plenty of time outside still, perhaps by including a cosy gathering area around a fire pit. Which of these easy tricks landscape designers use to carry a garden from fall into winter are right for your yard?

Adding a mix of ornamental grasses is a fundamental element of fall garden design and these low-maintenance plants will continue to look good all through winter. While many annual and perennial flowering plants will happily grow through airy grasses in summer, the blades will keep borders looking full once they've finish blooming.

Choose varieties that offer bold autumn color such as Panicum virgatum ‘Shenandoah’, available from Nature Hills. Also known as switch grass, this well-behaved clump-forming grass develops stunning red and damson tones in fall, topped by wiry stems of flowers. Reaching 3 feet high, it looks fabulous planted among taller shrubs as well as with perennial blooms.

Another option favored by landscape designers is blue-green-leaved Festuca glauca 'Elijah Blue', also available from Nature Hills. Growing to just a foot high, it's perfect for border edges and winter containers.

Landscape designers often choose trees with fiery foliage to create a stunning focal point with brilliant shades of scarlet, russet, gold or burgundy. Even if space is limited, there are plenty of smaller trees that will squeeze into a compact garden.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some of most spectacular fall color is typically associated with Acer (maple) trees, but to carry the interest on into winter, choose a type with textural bark, too. Acer griseum, the paperbark maple and available from Plant Addicts, has peeling, papery warm-brown bark. Caught in the light of a low winter sun, its peeling curls of bark are nothing short of spectacular. The coral bark Japanese maple, available from trees.com, has bark in an intense red tone that's equally eye-catching.

Another option if you're wondering what to plant in fall is a multi-trunked tree that, once the bright foliage has fallen, brings architectural interest to your garden, like the Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry tree, available from trees.com.

Attractively planted container gardens are a landscape designer's best friend during the cooler months of the year. These portable pots of color and texture can be positioned wherever you want, adding a welcoming touch to an entrance or a bright splash to a patio table.

There are all sorts of vibrant plants that love life in a patio pot and last from fall into winter for a wonderful cool-season display. The go-to formula is to combine a thriller (height), filler (body) and spiller (edging) to create a full, textured look. Good choices for fall and winter include compact evergreens or ornamental grasses to add the height element, pansies to fill out the body of the planter, and ivy to tumble over the edges. For a modern look, squeezing a container full of a single variety is an even easier option.

Dwarf pine trees are enjoying a surge in popularity with landscape designers, and no wonder. While in spring, summer and fall they provide a green, textural foil to colorful flowers and leaves, once winter arrives they emerge as standout sculptural shapes. The beauty of slow-growing dwarf pines is that they naturally stay compact and well-shaped, so need very little looking after.

Dwarf Mugo pine (Pinus mugo var. pumilo) is a particular favorite thanks to its dense, dark needles. While it eventually grows to 3-5 feet high, its easily kept pruned into a neat mound. Dwarf Mugo pine, available from trees.com, keeps its seed cones all through winter, adding to the display. Adding one, or an odd number dotted through your outside space, is a great way to ensure your garden has character throughout the year, and helps avoid that sensation of sparseness that often happens in winter when many plants are dormant.

When summer perennials and annuals fade you will need something else to take their place. Autumn-flowering bulbs will pop up reliably year after year to add color and, if you choose the right sunny spot, will naturalise, gently spreading to reflect how comfortable they are in your landscape. This repetition will strengthen the planting design, as well as adding continuity.

Nerine bowdenii (also known as as Bowden lily) brings an explosion of color to rejuvenate tired fall borders. These beautiful bright blooms on sturdy stems grow to 24 inches, and can be added to pots as well as planted in drifts through a flowerbed. In addition to the standard pink petals, there are varieties from white through to a deep ruby red, and Dutch Grown stocks a good nerine selection. While it's too late to plant the bulbs this year, you can pre-order ready for planting in spring for floral fireworks next fall.

Another favorite is hardy cyclamen, which you'll likely find potted at your local garden center in fall. Plant a mix of the hardy ivy-leaved cyclamen (Cyclamen hederifolium), which flowers in fall and has pretty foliage that lasts through winter, and winter-flowering cyclamen (Cyclamen coum) which blooms winter into spring, for a long season of interest.

Even during the cooler months of the year, your outdoor space should be an inviting spot where you want to linger. A fire pit creates an ambient spot to gather around at dusk offers the opportunity for year-round entertaining, and is a go-to for landscape designers interested in creating an outdoor space with year-round usability.

Whether you want the crackle of real wood burning or the convenience of starting a fire with the click of a button, a fire pit will add visual as well as physical warmth to your fall and winter garden. Opt for a design that complements your overall aesthetic and add layers of textured cushions and throws in a palette of warm, earthy tones to garden furniture to build on the cozy vibe.

This fire pit is perfect for patio evenings, bringing friends and family together around a warm, inviting flame. Though it burns real wood, an airflow system facilitates efficient combustion to reduce smoke levels.

Fuelled by wood or wood pellets, this 7-inch diameter stainless steel mini fire pit brings the s'mores experience to a patio table. Efficient burning means it's smokeless and a removable ash pan makes clean-up easy.

Fuelled by propane gas, this stylish fire pit has an adjustable flame and can deliver plenty of warmth to keep your outdoor gatherings cozy. A lid lets it double as a coffee table and it's also available in black and stone-look.

Landscape designers often use a mix of materials to maximize texture and interest in garden design. These are automatically thrown into the spotlight during the cooler months of the year when plants die back and leave the hardscaping exposed. Gravel offers a softer alternative to bare paving slabs, and buff-toned pea gravel in mixed sizes and shapes like this landscaping pea gravel from Lowe's creates a particularly natural look.

Softening the edges of hard landscaping with plants is another landscape-designer trick that comes into its own as a garden moves from fall into winter. Use evergreen creeping thyme to blend the edges of a curving pathway and a functional garden element becomes an attractive winter feature. You can also use gravel as a mulch to avoid areas of bare border soil in winter, an option that's also easy on the budget.

Another way to maximise texture and help your garden transition from fall into winter without missing a beat is to add warm lighting from a low angle. In fall, a ground-stake spotlight will highlight foliage but then is easily moved to throw a glow through ornamental grass blades. Even a wash of light across a gravel path creates a play of shadows that shows off texture to the full, and allows you to appreciate your garden from indoors on dark evenings.

The easiest way to create individual pools of low light is with solar spotlights, although you'll need to shop smart when buying outdoor solar lights that will generate enough power in fall and winter. For a start, choose lights with adjustable solar panels so they can be angled to match the sun's lower position in the sky. Look for a high conversion rate and a large capacity battery of at least 1500 mAh, too, and opt for warm-toned LEDS that will create more ambiance than bright white lights. These Solar Spot Lights from Wayfair tick all three boxes.

Lifestyle journalist Sarah Wilson writes about garden design and landscaping trends. She has studied introductory garden and landscape design, and also has an RHS Level 2 qualification in the Principles of Plant Growth and Development. She is a regular contributor to Homes & Gardens and Livingetc. She has also written for Country Living, Country Homes & Interiors, and Modern Gardens magazines.

#7823. When Art Meets Animal Rescue: A Creative Way to Help Dogs Find Homes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

Explore The Rescue Collection, use its rescue-finding tool to search by city or postcode, or meet dogs waiting for homes through The Sato Project.

#7822. Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box Review 2026: Our Expert’s Opinion

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

We give the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box a rating of 4.8 out of 5 stars.

Automatic litter boxes are not just a serious time saver for cat owners; theyâre also hugely beneficial for cats, particularly those that refuse to use anything but a fresh bed of cat litter. Yet, some cat parents are hesitant about the idea of bringing home a self-cleaning litter box.

For cats accustomed to an airy, open litter tray, a compact, closed-in automatic litter box might seem like too much of a change. But itâs not always just the cat that has to be convinced. For those accustomed to the simplicity of a basic litter tray, the idea of one with a power cord and moving parts may feel a bit overwhelming.

Whether your hesitation for buying an automatic litter box comes from your fears or your catâs, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box has you covered. This unique self-cleaning litter box is designed with an open-air feel to accommodate both large and claustrophobic kitties, and its âsafe by structureâ will give nervous owners total peace of mind.

I had a chance to test the new M9 with my big kitty, Makoa. Keep reading to find out if the clever design of this litter box really makes a difference in my full Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box review below.

In my experience, there are two big reasons cat parents hesitate to make the switch from a traditional litter pan to a fancy self-cleaning litter box.

The first reason is all about the cat. Many owners fear that their cat wonât be able to adjust to the design of an automatic litter box. While traditional tray boxes are wide open on top and allow plenty of room for big cats to turn around, dig, and stand tall as they do their business, most automatic boxes are more compact.

These boxes typically have hoods or are fully enclosed. Many also have smaller litter areas, which can be difficult for larger cats to navigate.

The second issue that keeps many parents scooping manually rather than investing in a box that can do it for them is about safety.

Automatic litter boxes have a lot of moving parts. Many turn completely upside down while cleaning, so itâs natural to be worried that your cat could be frightened, pinched, or trapped by the mechanism. Of course, these boxes have

sensors and safety controls to minimize the risks of an accident, but no technology is foolproof.

With their new automatic litter box, Neakasa listened to the most common concerns of hesitant cat parents and used them to inspire their design.

For the big or claustrophobic kitty, the M9 offers a wide-open, spacious design. The bowl-shaped hood isnât as open as a traditional pan without a roof, but the tilted angle and wide mouth make it much easier for large cats to navigate. And plenty of headspace means even big kitties like Maine Coons and Ragdolls can stand up tall while they do their business.

For the claustrophobic kitty, the M9 has another trick up its sleeve: the hood and âcabinâ of the litter box are translucent. This means plenty of light gets inside, and your cat has the ability to see all around them while they assume that oh-so vulnerable position.

The Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box also has plenty of reassuring features for even the most nervous owner.

This box has many of the same safety sensors that most other automatic boxes do. These work to prevent cleaning while the cat is present and stop cleaning if your cat leaps inside mid-cycle. But what makes the M9 different is that it is structurally designed to be safe even if those sensors fail.

Thanks to the spherical design and âtilt-safeâ rotation, even if the box were to somehow enter cleaning mode while your cat was inside, they would just get a bit of a ride (like a kitty in a hamster ball). Because the M9 cabin is free of pinch points and the opening does not close or shrink during cleaning, it would be virtually impossible for a cat to be harmed.

This is exactly the kind of fail-safe design nervous cat parents need.

Founded in 2017 as Neabot, Neakasa is a smart home and pet-care technology brand headquartered in Shenzhen, China, with offices in Los Angeles and Tokyo.

Its products aim to simplify everyday cleaning and pet care. Beyond automatic litter boxes, Neakasa offers pet grooming kits with vacuum technology, smart pet water fountains, and even air-purifying litter box steps.

As you can guess, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box is a great option for larger kitties and those who arenât likely to enjoy the cramped quarters of traditional automatic litter boxes. Itâs also great for safety-conscious owners.

But plenty of other cats and cat owners are likely to find something to love about this auto litter box option.

Thanks to the extra-large 1-liter odor control system, this litter box is a great choice for owners who want premium odor control in addition to automatic cleanup. The connected phone app and weight monitoring built into the box help track litter habits in single- and multi-cat households. Plus, the relatively compact footprint makes this box a good option for smaller spaces.

The M9 includes a long list of features that make it especially cat- and owner-friendly, including:

Automatic separation of clumped waste from reusable litter

Open-view design that provides visibility of the surroundings

Spacious cabin intended to accommodate a range of cat sizes

Easily removable components for routine cleaning

Multi-cat recognition and individual habit tracking

Automatic operation according to selected settings

Recommended clearance behind the unit: about 1.2â

Height needed for operation: about 27.2â

The Neakasa M9 works best with fast-clumping bentonite clay or mineral cat litter featuring uniform granules measuring approximately 2â4 mm. This size helps the machine sift clean litter from waste and collect clumps effectively. Crystal litter, tofu litter, and mixed litter are not recommended, as they may interfere with the automatic cleaning process.

The Neakasa M9 comes with everything needed to get started, including the litter box, a PureTower odor-control filter, a roll of 16 waste-drawer liners, five litter-emptying bags, and a power cord and adapter. It also includes a protective kitten guard, a quick-start guide, and a user manual.

Opening Size: 16.5â by 17.5â with transparent hood

Safety Features: Sensors plus tilt-safe design without pinch points or trapping potential

Odor defense: 1 liter PureTower filter with desiccant and activated carbon

My 12-pound Domestic Shorthair, Makoa, and I have tested a lot of automatic litter boxes in our time, and I can say with all honesty that the M9 from Neakasa is a true standout.

The litter box arrived in a rather large box with a somewhat overwhelming number of parts. But I promise you that it looks much harder than it is to put this together. Following the quick installation guide, I had it up and ready to go in less than ten minutes.

Insider tip: The installation instructions donât mention that the orange fixing ring (waste guide) at the back of the cabin must first be removed before the cabin can fit into the base.

I did have a bit of a problem getting the litter box to connect to my WiFi, which was interesting because I recently tested the Neakasa Riko Automatic Cat Feeder in the same room, using the same app, and had zero issues. But this could have just been an anomaly, because the next day I tried again and it connected right away.

Once the app was connected, everything was straightforward to set up. From there, it was hands-offâand Makoaâs time to test.

I set the M9 up in the laundry room next to his current automatic cat box, which is a more typical robot cat box with an enclosed cabin and full roof design. I know for a fact that Makoa prefers a more open design because he tends to stand up while he does his business and is a fairly large cat. Anytime he has a traditional litter pan available, he will always choose that over his current automatic litter box.

So it was no surprise to me that he immediately started using the M9 and didnât once use his old box during the testing period.

The step up into the M9 is a bit high. For smaller cats or those with mobility problems, I recommend checking out the Neakasa Air Step. I have one of these and ended up putting it in front of the M9 to catch litter, but Makoa definitely liked using it as a step as well.

In terms of odor control, cleaning prowess, and ease of use, this litter box performed exceptionally well.  As expected, the cleaning cycle stops if it senses weight or movement in the cabin, but I still really appreciate the smart design that makes it virtually impossible for a cat to get pinched or trapped if the safety sensors somehow failed and the cleaning cycle started while they were inside.

Overall, I have been really happy with this litter box, both in terms of its design and how well it cleans and reduces odors. More importantly, Makoa loves the larger space and open feel.

The 6-liter waste bin is advertised to last approximately 7â10 days for one cat, which I found to be pretty accurate. Households with multiple cats will likely need to empty it more frequently.

If youâve been hesitant to get an automatic litter box because you think your cat might not use it because itâs too cramped, or youâre worried about safety, I highly recommend looking into the Neakasa M9.

The thoughtful design eliminates both those concerns with an open, airy cabin and a unique structural design that removes pinch points and prevents trapping. Equally important, this smart litter box features powerful odor reduction, easily removable parts for cleaning, and an effective scooping system that gives you up to 10 days of hands-off operation.

If you're one of those people who spends a lot of time reading up on how to make your yard more appealing to your cats (or which plants that are poisonous for cats) rather than tips on how to repel the neighborhood's kitties, then chances are you've wondered which cat breed best matches your personality at least once. And after looking at our birth month pets, I couldn't resist taking a closer look at cats in particular...

I know, I know; we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month bird, birth month animal, birth month owl, and birth month bug, but cats are particularly brilliant if you want to match a critter up with your personality.

Whether you're a determined January baby, a dreamy June soul or a fiercely independent November personality, there's a feline to match your character. And so, from adventurous Bengals to affectionate ragdolls, here are all 12 birth months matched to the cat breeds that best capture their personality traits.

Grab yourself a packet of catmint seeds, then, and get ready to find out which cat matches your birth month...

If you're a January baby, you're known for being ambitious, independent and determined. It should come as no surprise, then, that the Maine Coon is your birth month cat; after all, these striking kitties have a confident presence, are intelligent and have a reputation for being independent-minded.

A natural leader of the cat world? Sound about right!

February belongs to the Abyssinian, which makes a lot of sense when you think about it. Just like the creative, curious and intelligent people born at this time of year, Abyssinians are famously inquisitive, playful and adventurous.

In other words, these kitties are true free spirits. Sound familiar?

March babies are quiet, sensitive and introspective – but don't let the fact that they're not the loudest in the room fool you. Especially as their birth month cat is an elegant beauty who's often reserved around strangers but affectionate with their trusted people.

Basically, the Russian Blue is a perfect match for March's gentle and imaginative personality for a reason. And, if this has struck a nerve with you, then why not honor your birth month cat further with this Russian Blue Calendar 2027?

Bold, adventurous and full of charisma, April belongs to one of the more unusual members of the cat family: the Bengal. Unlike many cats that absolutely abhor water, these pretty kitties absolutely love it – almost as much as they love exploring. This, coupled with their energetic and confident natures, means they're not exactly known for sitting quietly on the sidelines! (Sound familiar?)

One of the most iconic cat breeds going, May's birth month cat is the sociable, expressive and strong-willed Siamese.

With their bright blue eyes and unusual coloring, these kitties are among the most instantly recognizable breeds in the US. They're also famously vocal and people-oriented, with plenty of personality to keep everyone entertained... just like May babies.

If you're a June baby, you're romantic, sensitive and affectionate. No surprises, then, that your birth month cat is the beautiful ragdoll! These gorgeous kitties are known for their gentle souls, their people-loving natures and their tendency to follow their favorite humans around the house.

Essentially, they're a lovely fit for June's dreamy and sentimental side. And they go all floppy like a ragdoll when you pick them up, making them excellent snugglers, too!

If you're a July baby, you're curious, private and quietly determined – and you tend to prefer a small but loyal friendship group to a big and sprawling one. Enter, then, one of the cutest birth month cats on this list: the Birman!

Born in the height of summer, August babies tend to be every bit as sunny-natured as you think they'd be – think confident, outgoing and full of character. They certainly know how to command attention, and all hail that kind of chaotic energy, quite frankly!

September's long been associated with successful leaders, which means those born under this month tend to be practical, composed and deeply intelligent. Their birth month cats are similar, as British Shorthairs are generally calm, independent and undemanding.

They appreciate a routine and like things just so, but they like it that way for a reason – and it's why they're one of the most popular cats around, as it makes for a cuddly and serene companion.

October babies, assemble! While some might expect those born in the spookiest month of all to be assigned a birth month cat like the hairless Sphynx cat, think again!

Turkish Angoras are intelligent, playful and often quite determined. They have a flair for the dramatic, too, making them an ideal match for passionate, expressive and sociable October-born folk everywhere. (Although, admittedly, this 'I Like A Handful Of Humans And My Turkish Angora' Mug is giving pure Scorpio energy!).

If this is your birth month cat, you're mysterious, intuitive and quietly determined... and a brilliant person to have in anyone's corner, quite frankly.

Last but not least, December babies are known for being adventurous, energetic and fun-loving – and generous of spirit enough to be able to deal with the fact that their birthday falls smack-bang in the middle of the holidays.

Somalis, then, make their ideal birth month cat, as they are curious, playful and love exploring their surroundings. (As an added bonus, they're simply stunning, too!).

Ernest Hemingway famously declared that “a cat has absolute emotional honesty: human beings, for one reason or another, may hide their feelings, but a cat does not.” Whichever birth month cat you call your own, then, try to follow its good example and be more in touch with your true feelings and self.

Remember, too, that you don't have to own a cat (does anybody truly own a cat, after all?) to enjoy seeing them in your garden; plant up some cat-friendly plants, and watch the kitties go to town. Just be sure to keep bird feeders up and out of their way, yeah?

#7819. Susan’s Minnesota Garden, Part 2: Spring and Summer

Hi GPODers! We’re back in St. Paul, Minnesota (Zone 5a), for Part 2 of Susan Warde’s garden tour! Earlier this week, Susan shared a look at her garden from late July through October. Today we’re heading back to spring to see what was growing earlier in the season. Let’s take a look!

Here are some photos from late May through July.

The back garden. Wild cranesbill (Geranium maculatum, Zones 3–8) in the upper left corner is the only plant in flower at this time (late May), but the foliage is pretty, I think. The dominant hosta is ‘Blue Ivory’ (Hosta ‘Blue Ivory’, Zones 3–9).

Front garden (late May). I think the azalea is ‘Rosy Lights’ (Rhododendron ‘Rosy Lights’, Zones 3–7) from the Northern Lights azalea series.

Tall bearded iris (Iris ‘Cherished’, Zones 3–9), late May.

Tall bearded iris ‘Sultry Mood’, late May.

A Siberian iris (Iris sibirica cvs., Zones 3–9); I don’t know the cultivar name (late May).

My earliest clematis (Clematis ‘Acropolis’, Zones 4–9), with ‘Kansas’ peony (Paeonia lactiflora ‘Kansas’, Zones 3–8) in the background (early June).

This Asiatic lily (Lilium ‘Stracciatella Event’, Zones 3–8) was labeled ‘Stracciatella Event’, but it doesn’t look like the photos of that cultivar. Within a couple of days of this photo, taken July 6, the lily was demolished by scarlet lily beetles, which ultimately made mincemeat of all my lilies. The foliage looked so terrible that I had to cut them all down.

‘Lavender Moonchild’ daylily (Hemerocallis ‘Lavender Moonchild’, Zones 3–9), mid-July. Deer are a very rare occurrence in the city. I hadn’t seen one for years, but this summer two young bucks roamed the neighborhood, and every night they snacked on daylily buds and blossoms. They were not deterred by either of the sprays I tried.

This daylily is ‘Marquee Moon’. Set farther back in the garden, it was spared by the deer (mid-July).

A view of the side yard (July 25). Daylilies, garden phlox (Phlox paniculata cvs., Zones 4–8), coneflowers (Echinacea cvs., Zones 3–9), black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia cvs., Zones 3–9), and blazing stars (Liatris cvs., Zones 3–9) are all in bloom.

Thank you for sharing another look at your garden, Susan! I especially enjoyed seeing your collection of irises and daylilies, although I’m sorry the deer and lily beetles caused so much trouble this year.

If you missed Part 1, you can see Susan’s garden from late summer through fall.

#7818. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! Should I Use An Allergen-Neutralizing Spray? (November 2, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

#7817. Is That Really A Service Dog?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

What Your Christmas Cactus Needs in November – Ace These 4 Tasks for Fabulous Holiday Flowers

These 7 Plants Need Pruning Before Winter – November is Your Last Chance to Make the Cut
