Although hydrangea flowerheads can look pretty framed against a winter landscape, it’s important not to leave them to their own devices this month. Make a little time in November for these care essentials

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As November arrives, backyard activity may be slowing, but beneath the surface, hydrangeas are entering a critical transition. As day length shortens and the air gets fresher and nippier, deciduous shrubs shift their energy into the roots. Understanding exactly what to do (and not do) for hydrangeas now begins with recognizing that dormant plants are still susceptible to moisture stress and sub-zero cold.

Obviously, not all hydrangeas are the same. Some form buds on old wood, which means pruning now is a no-no. Other types are hardier than others, and so need less winter protection. So in order to give hydrangeas the best winter care, you must first know exactly which type of hydrangea you have. However, these November care tips can all help to make a big difference to next year’s display.

Taking action this month gives you enormous benefits in the approach to the colder months ahead. Taking time now can help you shield key dormant buds from bitter cold, adjust water levels, stabilize and protect roots, and ensure your plants emerge stronger than ever next spring. So don’t chance it and leave your favorite shrubs unattended this month. Here are the crucial tasks to do before winter…

Effective fall care lies primarily in knowing your hydrangea type and variety. Varieties that bloom on old wood, such as bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla) and oakleaf hydrangea (H. quercifolia) have already formed embryonic flower buds. If these buds freeze or are pruned off, next year's blooms will be tragically lost before you see them. Conversely, panicles (H. paniculata) and smooth hydrangeas (H. arborescens) produce flowers on new wood grown in spring, making them more resilient to frosts.

Popular bigleaf cultivars such as Nikko Blue or the Cityline series and serrated mountain hydrangeas need bud protection in cold zones. Cold-hardy panicle varieties like Limelight or Bobo and native smooth hydrangeas like Annabelle rarely require insulation, though they still benefit from consistent root hydration.

November hydrangea care also depends on your location, climate and USDA hardiness zone. Gardeners in northern zones 3-5 experience frozen ground and drying winter winds, demanding comprehensive stem barriers and thick thermal mulches. In contrast, those in southern zones 7-9 must contend with erratic temperature swings, where unseasonal late-fall warm spells can trick dormant buds into opening prematurely, only to be sheared by subsequent frosts.

Soil type also matters. Heavy clay soils hold water and risk winter ice pockets around roots, while light, sandy soils drain rapidly and dry out under frozen winds. Before tackling these tasks, it’s worth investing in a soil diagnostic tool with a long probe. The XLUX Deep Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, gives instant readings to make better decisions before the first hard freeze. Don’t forget your trusty bypass pruners to remove any dead or damaged branches safely, plus some isopropyl alcohol to clean blades before and after use. You’re then ready to start…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One of the kindest things you can do for your hydrangeas this month is to “think twice, cut once” when it comes to pruning. One of the biggest hydrangea mistakes is indiscriminately shearing back during fall cleanups. For old-wood bloomers like bigleaf, mountain, and oakleaf varieties, the buds that produce next summer’s flowers are already set near the tips of the stems. Pruning these in November removes those flower buds, reducing or eliminating next summer's blooms.

For these hydrangeas, you need to resist all structural shaping, topping, or cutting back until immediately after flowering finishes next year. The only exception is removing dead, diseased, or broken stems, which can be cut down to the base at any time. Use sharp bypass pruners like the Felco 2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, for exceptional clean cuts.

Equally important is leaving the faded, papery flower heads all winter long. While it might be tempting to tidy up dried flower clusters on varieties like Endless Summer or PeeGee, these old blooms act as shields for the tender buds tucked beneath them. So it’s a good idea to leave them in place now. Dried flower clusters also add visual interest to the winter garden, especially when they collect small mounds of snow. Then, in late winter or early spring, as fresh green growth emerges at the base, you can snip the old flower heads off above the first set of green buds.

Hydrangeas need plenty of water, even now. While deciduous foliage yellows and drops, hydrangea roots take up moisture until the soil drops below freezing. Winter air and winds can be drying, and with the ground frozen, the roots cannot replace what gets lost. So don’t be tempted to put your hoses and watering cans away too early. Entering winter in dehydrated soil can lead to brittle branches and dead tips by spring. Get your hydrangeas as hydrated as possible before winter really begins.

If you’re having a rainy fall, you might not need to water hydrangeas, but check the soil and give your hydrangeas a good soaking as needed. If rainfall is sparse, provide a deep, slow soaking every 10-14 days. Aim to moisten the soil 8-12 inches (10-15cm) deep, encouraging roots to settle deeper underground. Prioritize any newly planted shrubs, which need more water as they get established.

Soaker hoses are great options for targeted and controlled watering. You can buy Expert Gardener 50ft Soaker Hoses from Walmart to help you direct the flow wherever you grow your hydrangeas. Stop supplemental watering once morning frosts result in frozen soil.

Soil temperatures fluctuate erratically during late fall and early winter. Rapid freeze-and-thaw cycles cause frost heave, where expanding and contracting soil pushes shallow root crowns above the soil line, exposing roots to drying winds and freezing cold air. You can give key hydrangeas a helping hand by giving them extra insulation this month. This stabilizes soil temperatures, preserves deep moisture, and protects delicate roots through winter.

Start by adding a top-dressing of compost This will slowly break down over winter, releasing micronutrients that enhance soil and slowly feed the roots. A great composting option at this time of year is mushroom compost. You can get lush ready-made bags of Espoma Natural Mushroom Blend Fertilizer, from Walmart, to prime the earth and provide steady support through the colder months.

The compost can do double duty as an insulating mulch, but you can also use other types of mulch, like shredded bark or chopped leaves. Add a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose mulch. I like Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help lock in late-season soil moisture and regulate soil temperature. Always leave a 2-inch (5cm) gap around the woody stems to reduce the risks of fungal rot and gnawing rodents.

If you’re in zones 4-6 growing bigleaf or oakleaf hydrangeas, sub-zero cold and winter winds pose a big threat to next year's blooms. As noted, old wood hydrangeas have flower buds now. While the roots may be hardy to zone 5, flower buds can suffer frostbite below 0°F (-18°C). If stems die back, old-wood varieties will produce foliage during the summer, but zero flowers. So depending on your hardiness zones, consider adding some physical protection if your winters are very cold.

Do this in late November, after the plant drops its leaves and enters dormancy. Drive four sturdy hardwood or metal stakes into the ground around your hydrangea. Keep them several inches clear of the branches. Then wrap breathable fabric around the outside of the stakes to make a wind barrier. Use burlap or jute, such as Wellco Gardening Burlap Roll from The Home Depot, to protect against biting winds while maintaining healthy air flow around the plant. Secure with zip ties or twine.

For extreme northern climates, you can construct a cylinder of wire fencing around the plant and loosely fill with dry pine needles or oak leaves. Just avoid packing the leaves tightly and never use plastic tarps, which trap condensation and bake tender stems on sunnier winter afternoons.

Hydrangeas in outdoor pots, ceramic planters, and decorative troughs require proactive winter care. Unlike in-ground plants, potted roots are exposed to freezing air on all sides. An unprotected container's soil temperature can be 20°F lower than the garden soil, putting roots at risk of freezing and killing the plant outright. Ceramic and terracotta pots also absorb water, making them susceptible to cracking when wet soil freezes and expands. So you’ll need to give your container-based hydrangeas more protection if you have very cold winters.

Begin by grouping potted hydrangeas together along a sheltered, south or east-facing foundation wall, out of wind corridors. Elevate your pots off cold concrete using pot feet or bricks to ensure drainage holes remain clear. Wrap the body of each pot in bubble wrap, thermal burlap, or foam insulation, securing the wrap beneath the outer rim without covering the top soil. You can also pick up floating plant jackets or anti-frost fleece covers, such as the Valibe Shrub Protection Plant Jacket from Amazon, which you can slip over potted hydrangeas in cold snaps.

If you are in zone 6 or colder, move your potted hydrangeas into an unheated garage, garden shed, or cold frame for the winter. These sheltered spaces keep plants dormant while protecting them from sub-zero drafts. Check on them once a month, providing a splash of water so the roots never completely dry out.

As well as the things you should be doing this month, preparing your hydrangeas for the colder months requires knowing what to avoid. We’ve touched on pruning certain hydrangea types. Avoid aggressive pruning on old-wood varieties like bigleaf and oakleaf hydrangeas, which shears away next summer's flower buds. Another thing to avoid doing is allowing roots to dry out prior to ground freeze, as desiccated roots are vulnerable. Keep watering if the soil is dry and remains unfrozen.

Never apply high-nitrogen fertilizers at this time of year. Feeding now forces a flush of soft, tender growth that cannot harden off before freezing weather strikes, causing stem dieback. Don’t use clear plastic sheeting or non-breathable tarps as winter wraps, as they trap humidity, promote mold, and create greenhouse heat spikes on sunny days. This can trick dormant buds into waking prematurely. Finally, don’t just assume all hydrangeas need the same winter protection. Know your hydrangea type, how far north it is hardy, and how far you need to intervene to keep yours healthy.

Taking a little time in November to protect your hydrangeas makes all the difference for the year ahead. By maintaining hydration, shielding exposed old-wood buds from freezing gales, and insulating roots with a mulch blanket, you give your prized shrubs the exact winter protection they need. Come spring, your hydrangeas will emerge from dormancy strong, healthy, and ready to produce a summer display of blooms.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

#7814. “Love to the Point of Invention” – Injured Kitten with a Tiny Toy-Car Wheelchair Finds His Forever Home

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Some kittens steal your heart with their big eyes. Others win you over with their playful antics. And then there's Gelato, a tiny kitten who needed a wheelchair and ended up getting one made from Hot Wheels cars. Yes, really. Human ingenuity and humane creativity to the rescue!

Becoming more mobile in a Hot Wheels wheelchair might seem like a dream come true, but today, Gelato has even more reasons to celebrate: Heâs found his forever home.

Gelato arrived at Cincinnati Animal CARE in Ohio as a stray kitten with a lower-back injury that left him unable to use his hind legs normally. The shelter team wanted to help him move around, but there was a rather inconvenient problem. The wheelchairs they had available were too big for his tiny body.

Now, anyone who has lived with a kitten knows that, besides being irresistibly cute, they can be remarkably determined little creatures. They want to explore everything, investigate every corner, and get involved in whatever their humans are doing. Being unable to move around easily can limit those everyday experiences for the tiny fur balls.

Fortunately, Gelato had people in his corner who weren't about to let his small size stop him from exploring the big world.

The shelter's lead veterinary technician, Mallory Smith, came up with a wonderfully resourceful solution. She built a miniature wheelchair using cardboard, tape, zip ties, wooden rulers, and Hot Wheels toy cars. The first version needed adjustments, but Mallory kept working until the little device was ready to support Gelato as he moved around. While this is certainly quite a unique solution, what isnât unusual is the compassion and creativity behind it. Gelatoâs improvised mobility device is a perfect example of how animal medical care personnel go above and beyond to help patients in need.

Gelato's homemade wheelchair was a clever solution to an immediate problem. However, a makeshift device is not necessarily the best long-term option for a growing kitten with mobility challenges.

Help arrived in the form of an engineer who created a custom 3D-printed wheelchair designed to fit his body and accommodate his growth. The toy cars were gone, but Gelatoâs future mobility was looking more stable.

Gelato got lucky the moment someone refused to give up and asked, "How can we make this work?" This first lucky chance opened him to new opportunities from a wider effort to help one small animal have a better chance at life. Itâs impressive how sometimes sharing an animal's story can make all the difference. A social media post can connect shelters with people who have the skills, resources, or homes that animals need.

Giving Gelato a way to move around was an important first step. And there was another milestone waiting for him: a loving family of his own.

As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

Hollandsworth already cared for two cats with spinal injuries, Bread Crumb and Sprinkles. Both have limited use of their hind legs and rely on their front legs for mobility. She understood that caring for cats with special needs could involve extra responsibilities, adjustments, and plenty of patience.

In other words, she wasn't going into this adoption without knowing that life with a disabled cat can look a little different. Cat lovers are abundant, but those experienced in caring for disabled felines? Not quite as plentiful.

Hope wasted no time, adopting Gelato as soon as she met him at the shelter. The five-month-old kitten spent his first night in his new home sleeping in her arms.

Absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the company of people they trust.

What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

For a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Depending on the injury, a cat may need help with bladder or bowel function, regular skin checks, or a rehabilitation plan.

These are not small details. Some cats with spinal injuries cannot empty their bladders normally, which can lead to serious complications without very devoted care. A veterinarian can assess bladder function, mobility, sensation, and other concerns, then explain what support the cat will need at home. The real challenge is finding someone with the time and patience to take over these responsibilities on a daily basis.

Hollandsworth's experience with Bread Crumb and Sprinkles gave her a head start.

Gelato will continue receiving therapy in the hope that he may regain some use of his hind legs, but for now, his recovery is uncertain. Spinal injuries vary, and a cat's prognosis depends on several factors, including the extent of the damage and the neurological function that remains.

But Gelato doesn't need a guaranteed recovery to deserve a happy future. He's got somewhere to go, someone to cuddle, and absolutely no need to prove that he can walk to earn his place in the family.

His new family is ready to love and support him, whether or not he ever walks on his own. Hollandsworth put it beautifully: to her, Gelato is already perfect just the way he is.

There is a lot of wisdom in that simple sentiment. We can hope for progress, celebrate small improvements, and pursue appropriate treatment without making an animal's worth depend on how much they recover. Loving others, whether animals, people, or even ourselves, for who they are, exactly as they are, is what we call true love.

#7813. Halloween in the Garden: 3 Spooky and Creative Displays

Happy Friday, GPOD! Halloween is tomorrow, so for our last post of the week, I couldn’t resist digging through past GPODs for a little spooky-season garden inspiration. Over the years, contributors have shown us that Halloween decor doesn’t have to stop at the front door. A foggy morning can turn a familiar garden wonderfully eerie, homegrown pumpkins can become an entire cast of characters, and flowers and foliage from the garden can transform simple gourds into works of art. Today we’re revisiting three very different Halloween displays that all have their own charm and appeal.

We’ll start in Hebron, Kentucky, with Keri Shinault’s perfectly spooky garden. Keri and her husband, Brandon, began hosting an annual Halloween masquerade after their October 2005 wedding, eventually decorating their home and garden with creepy critters, ghouls, headstones, and plenty of other spooky surprises.

A beautiful sitting area surrounded by lush plants becomes instantly more mysterious when fog blurs the garden beyond.

Sometimes Mother Nature provides the best Halloween special effects.

Sit a while! Take a load off those tired bones.

Stepping stones set into lush ground covers guide you around massive oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia, Zones 5–9) shrubs.

Next up are Tom and Jeannie Tremont’s delightfully ridiculous pumpkin people. Rather than simply lining the porch with gourds, Tom and Jeannie turned their pumpkins into an entire cast of characters with their own poses, props, and personalities.

Why settle for a jack-o’-lantern when your pumpkins can go for a bike ride? Tom and Jeannie turned their fall harvest into a whole cast of characters, complete with wheels.

Tom and Jeannie Tremont clearly weren’t interested in ordinary jack-o’-lanterns. This pumpkin person looks like they got caught with their pants down while a family bikes by in the background. It’s ridiculous in the best possible way.

The mama-and-baby pumpkin pair might be the sweetest of the bunch. Even commenters on the original GPOD singled this little duo out as a favorite.

We’ll end with something completely different from Cherry Ong in Richmond, British Columbia. For her dazzling pumpkin display, Cherry repurposed the pallet-wood auricula theaters she and her husband had built for spring into a stage for decorated pumpkins and squash.

Auricula theaters traditionally protect auriculas (Primula auricula, Zones 3–8) from harsh rain and wind, but Cherry discovered they make a pretty spectacular fall display too.

Cherry and her husband built these pallet-wood auricula theaters a couple of years earlier—he constructed and hung the boxes, while Cherry designed and stained them. In fall, the shelves get a totally new look when pumpkins and gourds take the place of spring flowers.

Cherry had a little fun displaying the smaller pumpkins before giving them away, using old mini terra-cotta pots to add height and variation. Some pumpkins were decorated with seasonal flowers and foliage from the garden, turning the whole theater into one big botanical arrangement.

A small white pumpkin topped with clusters of Chinese tea rosebuds shows just how detailed Cherry gets with these creations. Elsewhere in the display, she also incorporated dried dahlias and other flowers and foliage from the garden.

I love how each of these gardeners found a unique way to bring Halloween into their outdoor spaces. That might be my favorite thing about Halloween in the garden: there really aren’t many rules. You can go creepy, silly, beautiful, botanical—or somehow all four at once. I hope everyone has a happy Halloween tomorrow! If you’re decorating your garden, porch, containers, or homegrown pumpkins this weekend, I’d love to see what you come up with.

Hidden in plain sight in the posters and trailers, these 12 plants could reveal more than you think about The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's something about Suzanne Collins' iconic dystopian series that feels more relevant than ever, and, with the latest film taking us back to the 50th Hunger Games, there's plenty for fans to scrutinize beyond the action itself. Personally, though, I can't stop looking at the plants.

If you've followed the franchise, you'll know that nature has never been merely decorative in Panem. From sinister plants and poisonous berries to the natural world providing food, healing plants, and shelter, knowing your botany in the arena can quite literally mean the difference between life and death.

There's also a long literary tradition of using plants as an act of resistance. After all, flowers have carried hidden messages for centuries, from the symbolism of roses in mythology to the elaborate Victorian language of flowers, when a carefully chosen bouquet could communicate everything from secret affection to heartbreak.

Watch The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Trailer:

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Even the names of some of the franchise's most memorable characters have botanical connections. Katniss is named after Sagittaria latifolia, a real North American aquatic plant also known as a swamp potato thanks to its edible tubers – making it a rather fitting namesake for a character whose survival instincts are so closely connected to the natural world.

Rue, meanwhile, shares her name with an aromatic herb traditionally associated with regret and sorrow (which is heartbreaking when you consider her story). And it seems the trailers and posters for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping suggest that the franchise's botanical language is far from finished.

From wildflowers carpeting the arena to carefully arranged floral displays around some of Panem's most recognisable characters, there are plenty of plants worth looking twice at in the posters and trailers alike.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some have fascinating historical meanings, others have surprisingly sinister botanical properties, and more than a few might offer clues about the story's characters and themes.

With that in mind, then, here are 12 botanical details I've spotted – and what they could mean.

The striking urn plant, Aechmea fasciata, is a popular bromeliad that's hard to miss in the above Sunrise On The Reaping poster thanks to its architectural rosette of silvery-green leaves and bright pink flower spike.

Its name comes from the distinctive cup formed by its overlapping leaves, which collects water in its natural habitat. This adaptation helps the plant make the most of the resources around it, even when growing conditions are challenging.

It's easy to see why it makes an interesting symbol in the Hunger Games universe. Urn plants are associated with resilience, adaptation and protection – qualities that are essential when survival is the ultimate prize. There's something particularly fitting about a plant that creates its own little reservoir of resources in a world where nothing comes easily, right?

Foxgloves (Digitalis purpurea) are among Britain's most recognisable wildflowers. Their tall flower spikes and bell-shaped blooms make them a favourite with pollinators and cottage garden enthusiasts... but there's a darker side to these pretty flowers. Every part of the foxglove plant is poisonous, containing compounds called cardiac glycosides that affect the heart.

Interestingly, those same compounds have played an important role in medicine. Digitalis-derived drugs have been used to treat certain heart conditions, making foxgloves a fascinating example of how the line between medicine and poison can depend on the dose.

In the Hunger Games, then, foxgloves could represent the duality of healing and danger – something that feels particularly at home in an arena where even the most beautiful things can be deadly.

White roses have long been associated with innocence, purity and remembrance. In Victorian flower dictionaries, their meanings included innocence, silence and even a holy death. Their appearance around President Snow is therefore particularly interesting, especially considering he's one of Panem's most ruthless figures.

Could they be a visual reminder of the innocence destroyed by the Capitol? Or perhaps a suggestion that even the most pristine-looking things can conceal something rotten underneath?

If white roses suggest purity, red roses are traditionally associated with passionate love and desire. They have been used for centuries as declarations of affection, but their symbolism isn't always straightforward. In the Victorian language of flowers, different shades and arrangements could carry different messages, from deep devotion to longing.

When red roses appear around President Snow, it's difficult not to consider the contrast between romantic passion and the bloodshed associated with his regime. After all, their vivid color also makes them an interesting counterpart to the white roses. Together, then, the two colors create a visual language of innocence, passion, power and mortality... which is very Hunger Games-coded.

The California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is instantly recognisable by its bright orange flowers. Native to western North America, it's also the official state flower of California. It's a hardy plant that thrives in sunny conditions and can tolerate relatively poor soils, making it a lovely symbol of resilience.

Poppies have different meanings across cultures, but they're frequently associated with remembrance, sleep and renewal. The California poppy's connection to the American landscape, though, makes it particularly interesting in the world of the Hunger Games, especially as it reimagines a future North America as Panem... especially as its bright and cheerful appearance feels so ironic against the darker world in which the Games take place.

Try the Burpee Sunset Mixed California Poppy Flower Seed from Walmart if you're in the mood for shades of orange, yellow, and cream in your own garden. You can even sow the seeds directly into gravel or cracks, too!

If you've spotted the sunflowers in the character poster for Percy Daggs IV as Ampert, you're not alone in wondering what they mean for the new Hunger Games film. After all, it's difficult to look at a sunflower (Helianthus annuus) without thinking of sunshine, happiness and optimism.

These towering annuals are often associated with hope, loyalty and resilience. Their ability to grow quickly and produce impressive flower heads makes them a familiar symbol of strength and positivity, and there's also a lovely modern interpretation of sunflower symbolism that centers on community and supporting one another through difficult times.

In a story where alliances can mean survival? Well, that sense of solidarity feels particularly poignant.

Canterbury bells (Campanula medium) are charming cottage garden flowers with tall stems covered in nodding bell-shaped blooms. And, fun fact, they're also the birth month biennial for May babies, too!

Their traditional Victorian flower meaning was 'acknowledgement', while other historical dictionaries associated them more generally with constancy. And, in a story about loyalty, friendship and the people we stand alongside when times get difficult, both interpretations feel rather fitting.

Celebrate the Tributes' attempt to break the machine, then, with a packet of Canterbury Bells Double Mix from Amazon.

The unusual pincushion protea, from the genus Leucospermum, has an unmistakable appearance. Its spiky flower heads look almost like elaborate fireworks or, as the name suggests, a pincushion.

Native to southern Africa, these evergreen shrubs are adapted to challenging growing conditions and are known for their striking flowers. Proteas more broadly, though, have become associated with transformation, strength, courage and diversity. As such, their unusual appearance also makes them a natural symbol of individuality.

Their presence around Effie Trinket is a possible nod to her flamboyant personality, as Effie has always been someone who embraces color, extravagance and standing out from the crowd, even when the world around her is anything but cheerful. Peersonally, though, this writer thinks it might be a nod to her eventual character arc...

Toadstools might not technically be plants – they're fungi, as we made very clear in our recent piece on birth month mushrooms – but they deserve a place in this botanical spotter's guide.

Fungi are essential to healthy ecosystems, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil. Some species, however, are highly poisonous, while others have medicinal or mind-altering properties, and that contrast gives mushrooms a fascinating symbolic role. They can represent decay and death, but also renewal, transformation and altered states of consciousness.

In the world of the Hunger Games, where the natural environment is often manipulated to confuse, frighten or kill its inhabitants? I suspect toadstools are a fitting reminder that not everything growing in the wild should be trusted.

Bee balm (Monarda) is a North American perennial loved by bees, butterflies and hummingbirds. Its colorful and nectar-rich flowers (particularly this stunning Pocahontas Purple Rose Bee Balm from Nature Hills) make it a wonderful addition to pollinator-friendly gardens, while the plant also has a history of traditional herbal use.

Today, bee balm is sometimes associated with compassion, empathy and comfort during difficult times. An RHS study of historical flower dictionaries, however, reveals that one nineteenth-century interpretation of this super-spreader was rather less affectionate: "Your whims are quite unbearable".

That's quite a contrast to the modern associations of care and kindness – and makes its appearance in the sinister world of the Hunger Games all the more intriguing... especially for those who remember the role they played in the Sunrise On The Reaping book.

Now here's a botanical detail I particularly love, as Nepenthes is a genus of tropical carnivorous plants, commonly known as tropical pitcher plants. Their distinctive modified leaves form hanging pitchers filled with digestive fluid, which trap and break down insects and other small prey.

The genus name has a fascinating origin. It comes from the Greek word nepenthes, associated with a mythical substance that banished sorrow or grief, which is an extraordinary name for a plant that catches and digests its victims.

In the context of the Hunger Games, the contrast is almost too good to ignore. A plant whose name evokes freedom from grief, but whose survival strategy involves trapping and consuming other creatures? Surely that's a dark metaphor for Panem itself (and almost worth buying a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Storein the run-up to the film, too).

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Spanish bluebells (Hyacinthoides hispanica) are popular spring-flowering bulbs, producing upright stems covered in clusters of blue, pink or white bell-shaped flowers. Unlike native blooms, though, these can spread vigorously in gardens and hybridize with native bluebells – something which hhis has raised concerns about the genetic integrity of native woodland populations.

The resulting hybrids can be difficult to identify, and experts advise gardeners living close to native bluebell populations to avoid planting Spanish bluebells. In terms of the Hunger Games, then, it's an interesting possible metaphor for displacement, hybridization and the arrival of an outsider that changes an established ecosystem.

In a story so concerned with power, territory and the destruction of existing communities, it feels like an idea well worth considering.

Beyond the individual plants seen across the posters and trailers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, it's the wider meadow-like landscape of the arena that deserves attention.

Wildflowers are usually associated with freedom, biodiversity and the natural world growing without human interference, and tend to evoke a sense of peace and escape from the pressures of modern life. This arena, though, turns that idea on its head, forcing nature to become a part of the spectacle. Its beauty is carefully presented, but the environment is ultimately controlled by the Gamemakers. A field of flowers might look like an idyllic meadow, yet it exists within a space designed to test, manipulate and endanger the tributes.

It's a clever contrast between the natural world as something beautiful and life-giving, and nature as something that can be manipulated into a weapon. And perhaps that's the biggest botanical message of all: in Panem, you should never assume that anything is harmless. Even something as simple and innocuous as, say, a flower.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7811. Is Your Dog Weird Enough for Times Square?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Does your pup have a bedtime routine that makes no sense, a suspicious obsession with household objects, or dramatically howl at their own reflection in the oven door? Congratulations. You might be living with a contender for the World's Weirdest Dog. Embark Veterinary has officially launched its search for canine oddballs, inviting pet parents to submit photos and videos of their furballâs most gloriously bizarre behaviors before November 15, 2026. The winning pup will earn the ultimate claim to canine fame: their face on a Times Square billboard, the official title of World's Weirdest Dog, and a $200 gift card.

The contest celebrates the behaviors that make dogs funny, unique, and truly memorable; the ones that make us smile when we think about them, while also highlighting  Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature, which explores how canine DNA may influence behavior.

Sock Thieves, Bathtub Sleepers, and Other Household Oddballs

Furry weirdos have interesting, different habits; Embark's examples include a dog who sleeps upside down in the bathtub, one who carries a sock around without chewing it, and a canine who spins exactly three times before lying down. Not two. Not four. Three.

Then there's the dog who refuses to walk past one particular house, or the dinner diva who won't touch a meal until someone has given it the full restaurant treatment.

Such behaviors are entertaining partly because they are so unique and specific. Most pet parents can share at least one story that would make a perfectly reasonable person wonder what goes on inside that furry little head.

A sock might be a very treasured object, a source of comfort, a reminder of their favorite personâs scent, or simply something fun to carry. A particular walking route might feel uncomfortable for reasons a person cannot detect, most likely a scentâ¦ but then again, who knows? And a bedtime ritual may have started with nothing more mysterious than finding a comfortable position.

Of course, some dogs are just little weirdos, and that's part of their charm. But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. If your pup begins staring at walls, repeating the same movements, or turning down food when that's not normal for them, don't automatically label it as a new amusing personality trait. Pain, illness, and anxiety can all show up as changes in behavior. If something feels off, put the camera down and call the vet.

Genes can influence behavioral tendencies, but they don't write a complete script for an individual dog's life. Learning and environment play a big role, too, sometimes in ways pet parents never intended.

Take the sock thief. A dog grabs a sock, their pet parents react with dramatic excitement, and suddenly the household is involved in a thrilling chase. From our perspective, it's a laundry crime. From the pup's perspective, it may be an excellent new game.

Behaviors that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes are more likely to happen again. Attention, play, food, and access to preferred activities can all reinforce behavior, even when nobody is training anything on purpose.

Genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

Some dogs may be especially motivated to retrieve, chase, or investigate, reflecting tendencies shaped partly by their ancestry and breeding history. But individual dogs still vary, and experience helps shape how those tendencies appear. However, with more data, we may learn new things; science is ever evolving along with our technologies.

Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature connects genetic information with behavioral insights and training guidance. Genetic results can be useful, but they are one piece of the puzzle and not a personality prediction.

Behavior is best understood in context. Has the habit been present for years, or did it start last week? What happens before the behavior? Could pain, fear, stress, or another medical issue be contributing?

If a pup is safe and comfortable, there's often no reason to stop a peculiar routine unless itâs a problem. A dog who carries a favorite toy around the house doesn't need a corrective training plan. When a behavior does create a problem, redirection and positive reinforcement can help teach an alternative response without relying on intimidation or punishment. This is the science of behavioral modification.

The goal isn't to turn every pup into a perfectly polished obedience champion, but to help us understand what each dog needs and help them become great family members.

Pet parents can enroll their weirdos through November 15, 2026, by uploading a photo or video of their pup's strangest behavior, with an optional short story, at Embark's official contest page. No weird dog? No problem. You can still get involved by casting your vote for the weirdest dog through the official voting page.

The first-place winner will receive the World's Weirdest Dog title, a Times Square billboard feature, and a $200 gift card. Second through fifth place will receive $150 gift cards each, while sixth through fifteenth place will receive an Embark Breed + Health Dog DNA Test with the Behavior Insights & Training upgrade.

So, if you know your furry pal is a weirdo, this may be their moment. Let that freak flag fly!

#7810. Diagnosing a Ghost – The Mysterious Feline Disease Whose Signs Appear & Disappear

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go. A cat that is on deathâs door one moment, running around the next. Detecting illness in cats can be difficult enough, but when the body starts attacking itself, diagnosis becomes even more of a challenge.

In an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect. Fortunately, autoimmune disease is relatively uncommon in cats, but it can be serious and difficult to diagnose and treat. Because the signs tend to be vague and can come and go, they are easy to overlook, which makes it worth knowing what to watch for and when to involve a vet.

A healthy immune system protects the body from germs such as viruses and bacteria by sending out specialized cells to locate and destroy them. It also helps clear away damaged or diseased cells. These immune cells use protein signals on the surface of the bodyâs own cells to recognize them as safe. In autoimmune disease, a signaling error causes the immune system to treat the catâs own cells as a threat, and healthy, working tissue gets attacked and destroyed.

Cats can develop these problems much as people do. They can affect any part of the body, including the internal organs, blood, and skin, and there are many different types. Some can be life-threatening, weakening the bodyâs natural defenses while also damaging healthy tissue.

The part of the body under attack determines which signs appear, so the picture varies dramatically from one cat to the next. Signs are often general and not immediately linked to an autoimmune problem. Possible signs include lethargy, weakness, decreased appetite, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and other changes to the feces. Other signs include pale gums, unexplained bleeding, bruising, a high temperature, a faster heart rate, rapid breathing, and tiring easily during play. Limping, swollen joints, sores on the skin, a poor coat, increased thirst, increased urination, and collapse are also on the list.

Many of these signs come and go. A cat may seem completely fine one day and be struggling the next. Any of these signs are a reason to contact a vet promptly, since starting investigations early makes a real difference.

The problem starts with the catâs own immune system, which is part of what makes it so hard to manage. The exact triggers are not fully understood, and more research is needed. An immune-mediated condition can be triggered when the immune system is stimulated. Viral infections, vaccination, medications, inherited conditions, and hormones have all been linked to autoimmune disease. Where things get tricky is that the incident that triggered the disease is not usually the cause of the disease. That means that the same type of autoimmune disease can be triggered by different things in different individuals.

Some of these conditions can be passed down, and other possible contributors include poor nutrition, toxins, cancer, and stress. A cat diagnosed with an autoimmune disease considered hereditary should not be bred under any circumstances.

Diagnosis is often a process of elimination. More common causes of the same signs are investigated and ruled out first, which can mean lots of tests. A vet will start with a full physical exam and a detailed history, then choose tests to fit the signs. These may include blood and urine tests, X-rays, or an ultrasound scan. Samples may also be taken from wounds, rashes, or other affected areas. Prompt diagnosis is important for effective management.

Treatment depends on the type of autoimmune disease, what part of the body is affected, and what is behind it, so it varies greatly. The usual approach is medication that calms the immune system so it stops attacking the body, most often corticosteroids like prednisone or dexamethasone. A large starting dose is often given, and once the signs settle down, the dose is lowered gradually.

Sometimes, stronger immunosuppressive drugs are also used. Some of them are also used in cancer treatment, and the side effects tend to be more severe. The trouble with treating an immune-mediated disease is that we are using medication to suppress the immune system, and that leaves the patient more susceptible to infection and other diseases.

Even more challenging when treating feline autoimmune disease is that some of the medications used to treat dogs or humans are toxic to cats.

Supportive care matters just as much. Pain relief is often needed, but many commonly prescribed anti-inflammatory painkillers cannot be given alongside steroids. Stronger painkillers like opioids or gabapentin may be used to manage severe pain, and these come with their own side effects. Antibiotics may also be prescribed, either prophylactically if extremely high doses of immunosuppressive medications are being used, or if secondary infections develop.

For cats with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), where the immune system is attacking and destroying red blood cells, or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP) where platelets are being destroyed, blood or plasma transfusions may be needed to save a catâs life.

Lifestyle changes can help too. A cat with painful, swollen joints, for example, benefits from losing weight if overweight, and lower sides on litter trays and softer beds make life more comfortable. Each case is assessed individually.

One of the more common autoimmune diseases in cats is known as Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex, a group of idiopathic conditions that are currently quite poorly understood. The exact cause of the disease is unknown; however, parasites, allergies, and genetic factors have been identified as likely triggers.

There are three main clinical presentations of eosinophilic granuloma complex:

Ulcerative: Also known as indolent ulcers or rodent ulcers, this form of eosinophilic granuloma complex usually presents with a sore on the cat's mouth. It is typically seen on the upper lip. They are normally red in color and do not appear to cause your cat any pain or irritation.

Plaque-forming: often found on the stomach and on the inside of the hind legs. The lesions are often itchy and red and often become infected, which complicates matters.

Granuloma forming: usually presents as raised pink or yellow nodules that can be located anywhere on your cat.

Another more common feline immune-mediated disease is called pemphigus foliaceus. It affects the skin, causing scabs, crusts, and sores around the eyes and ears, on the paws, and in the groin area. When it develops on the paws, the nail beds can be affected as well.

There is no cure for autoimmune disease, but effective treatment and management can control the signs, greatly improve quality of life, and allow most cats to live fairly comfortably. These conditions can be debilitating and life-threatening, yet it is often possible to manage them well enough for cats to lead relatively normal lives. Because the signs overlap with so many other conditions, a vet visit at the first sign that something is wrong is the surest way to get answers early.

#7809. Lights Out, Zoomies On: Why Dogs Go Wild at Bedtime

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

While nighttime zoomies are a well-recognized phenomenon in the feline world, it turns out dogs can also get a little over-excited at the prospect of bedtime. Just as the house is settling down for the night, a dog may start bouncing around, digging into the blankets, or demanding attention.

It also turns out that there isn't a single explanation for this evening burst of energy; there are several. The bed itself can be exciting, particularly because it smells like a favorite person and offers a chance for interaction. In other cases, a dog may simply have energy left to burn. Understanding the possible reasons can help explain why bedtime sometimes turns into playtime.

Dogs spend much of their time looking up at people from the floor. Climbing onto a bed changes that perspective, bringing a dog much closer to its owner's face and making interaction easier.

That alone can be enough to spark a playful mood. A dog may drop into a play bow, bark for attention, or bounce around in an attempt to encourage its person to join in.

Being face to face can make play feel more inviting, particularly for dogs that enjoy close interaction with their owners. What looks like a sudden burst of energy may simply be a dog making the most of the opportunity to engage on a different level.

A bed carries the scent of the person who sleeps in it, making it an especially interesting place for a dog to explore. Dogs rely heavily on their noses to understand their surroundings, and familiar smells can be particularly appealing.

For a dog that enjoys spending time with its owner, the bed may be one of the most comforting and interesting places in the home. Rolling around on the sheets or sniffing the blankets lets a dog investigate those familiar scents while enjoying a spot associated with its favorite person.

That combination of comfort, familiarity, and excitement can help explain why some dogs become especially playful once they climb onto the mattress.

For dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

Some breeds are particularly inclined toward this kind of behavior. Dachshunds, for example, were bred to pursue animals such as badgers and weasels into their burrows. Their instinct to dig and tunnel can make a pile of blankets especially appealing. Meanwhile, Chihuahuas seem to be particularly fond of burrowing into the warmth and security of their humanâs bed.

A dog that discovers the pleasure of diving between the sheets may quickly turn it into a regular bedtime activity.

Dogs are often quick to learn which behaviors get a reaction from their owners. Climbing onto the bed puts them right where they're difficult to ignore, particularly if they start bouncing around or nudging someone for attention.

Bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

If playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. What begins as a burst of excitement can become a familiar part of the nightly routine. Even if this nightly ritual isnât one you welcome, waving arms and raised voices often count as a positive interaction for a dog, so if youâre trying to get your dog off the bed, be careful your methods align with your message.

Sometimes, a dog becomes especially energetic at bedtime simply because theyâre not ready to settle down. If it hasn't had enough exercise or stimulation during the day, the bed may become an outlet for that leftover energy.

A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

Many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

There are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

Ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

If you do want your bed to be a dog-free zone, the simplest solution is to keep the bedroom door closed. But if youâre simply looking for a way to get them off the bed without it turning into a party, a calm and quiet approach is best. A single command or using a slip-lead to silently guide them off the bed will be far more effective than shouting and pointing.

A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

If the behavior seems excessive, however, it may be worth looking at how much exercise and stimulation the dog gets during the day. Adding a walk or play session before bed can help make the transition to sleep easier.

For many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

Those tiny black flies are only part of the story. A raw potato slice on the soil can reveal what's underneath for next to nothing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You water your houseplant, and a little cloud of tiny black flies lifts off the soil. A minute later, they're on the window. Fungus gnats turn up in many homes once fall arrives, and they can hang around all winter. The next batch is already growing in the pot, and a fungus gnat potato trap is an easy way to find them.

Before you read up on how to get rid of fungus gnats, take a look at what's going on in the pot. The adult flies you keep swatting don't feed on your plants, but their larvae are a different story. Those live in the damp potting mix just under the surface, out of sight unless you go digging.

One raw potato saves you the digging. Lay a slice on the soil, and the larvae come up to feed on it. Lift it a couple of days later, and whatever is in the pot is often feeding on the underside. Odds are there's a potato in the pantry already, so finding out costs you pretty much nothing, really.

A fungus gnat's whole life happens in or around the pot. They're small flies, often in the genus Bradysia, and a female can lay up to 200 eggs in damp potting mix. Once they hatch, the larvae eat for a couple of weeks and pupate near the surface, and new adults show up a week or so later. At room temperature, that's roughly three to four weeks per generation – so a few flies in October can be a lot more by the holidays.

It's the larvae doing the eating. Their usual food is fungi and rotting organic matter, but they'll go after fine root hairs too. While a minor infestation won't usually do any harm, enough of them can damage roots and stunt growth, especially in seedlings and young plants. Watch for something like a tiny worm: clear or whitish, no legs, a shiny black head, ¼ inch (6 mm) long at most.

Cut a raw potato into slices about ¼ inch (6.4 mm) thick. Set one cut side down on the potting mix, and press it lightly so it sits flat. That contact is the whole trick. Larvae move up to the potato as a food source and gather on the moist underside where it touches the soil.

Give it a day or two before the first look. Flip the slice and check its underside, then the soil where it sat, for tiny clear larvae. Against dark, wet potting mix, they're hard to pick out, though, so a magnifying glass, like this Rongon 10X folding pocket magnifier from Amazon, helps a lot. Nothing there yet? Set it back down for another day or two. Sometimes larvae can take a few days to find the potato.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Don't leave it there for good, though. Raw potato breaks down in damp soil, and a rotting slice is just more of the decaying material larvae feed on. Toss the old one in the trash, larvae and all, and put down a fresh slice. Used like this, potato slices for fungus gnats let you track whether the numbers are dropping. Eggs won't show up on it. They don't feed, so they stay put in the mix.

So, do potatoes kill fungus gnats? Not really. The potato doesn't poison anything – it just draws feeding larvae up from the roots, and tossing a slice with larvae on it removes those ones. Eggs, pupae, and the adults flying around the room aren't affected.

Use the potato to check on things, then reach for something else to fix it. Say the slice comes up clean. That's nice, but it doesn't mean the pot's clear. Maybe there are only a few larvae, or they weren't feeding much. If flies keep hanging around, put down another slice.

Too much water keeps a lot of fungus gnat problems going. Short days and cool rooms slow houseplants down in fall and winter, so they use less water. Water like it's still July, and the mix stays wet, which eggs and larvae love. Let the top inch (2.5cm) dry before watering again. Empty the saucer, and make sure the pot drains. Old mix holds extra water as it breaks down. If a plant's due for repotting, look for a fresh mix with perlite for drainage, like the Back to the Roots Indoor Potting Mix, available from Walmart.

Yellow sticky traps are for the adults. Push a few into the pot – you can buy sticky traps cheaply from Amazon. Each female stuck to one won't lay any more eggs, and the count tells you if things are improving. Down in the soil, the larvae aren't touched. If the gnats won't let up, try Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis), a naturally occurring soil bacterium. Despite the name, it isn't the Bt sprayed on caterpillars. This strain targets only fly larvae.

Summit Mosquito Bits use Bti to control both mosquito and fungus gnat larvae. Rather than scattering the granules on the soil, it's best to soak them in water for about 30 minutes, then apply that water to your houseplant soil. Repeat application about every five days, since Bti doesn't last long indoors.

Beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae), such as BioLogic's Scanmask nematodes, are another organic option. These microscopic roundworms seek out fungus gnat larvae in potting soil. They enter the larvae and release bacteria that kill them, then feed and reproduce inside their bodies. It's pretty gruesome, but effective. They arrive alive in the mail, so use them right away. Keep the soil moist and the temperature between 60 and 90°Fahrenheit (16–32°C), or they won't work. Whichever you buy, check that the label allows indoor potted plants, then follow it.

Catching larvae early makes a fungus gnat problem much easier to control. A few larvae in one pot make for a far smaller job than a houseful of flies a month from now – and a potato slice is a cheap way to see whether your houseplant soil is hiding them.

So keep a potato around this winter. Set a fresh slice down whenever the flies show up again, and go easier on the watering while days are short. Fungus gnats have a much harder time of it once the top of the soil dries out between drinks!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7806. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us, but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s Zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I really like the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. And I’m with you on already thinking about spring—I’d love to see what you decide to grow over that new arch!

Yellowing leaves this month are usually caused by the #1 seasonal mistake houseplant parents make. Here’s how to save your plant's life before it’s too late.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your houseplant leaves are turning yellow this November, your plant is sending urgent distress signals that you really need to heed. As days shorten and sunlight becomes less intense in fall, most houseplants use far less moisture as their growth dramatically slows. Continuing your summer watering routine during this shift creates waterlogged soil, quickly leading to root rot – and an avoidable trip to the compost bin. Catch that first yellow leaf early, however, and you can quickly reverse the damage to keep your houseplant happy and healthy.

Failing to adjust a watering routine in line with houseplants’ seasonal needs is the most common mistake we plant parents make, and unfortunately the root rot that results can be fatal. It takes a few weeks of waterlogged soil and rotting roots before the damage manifests with yellowing leaves, which is why this symptom usually shows up in November – and why once you spot a yellowing leaf you need to take swift action.

So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a yellowing leaf, and save it from an untimely death with a simple fix.

Take a closer look at the yellow houseplant leaf to see what tone, shape, position and extent of the discoloration is. Different plants show this early symptom of root rot in various ways: a Monstera will likely get a yellow halo on one of its monster-sized leaves while a ZZ plant leaf will turn bright yellow from top to bottom overnight. Peperomia foliage typically fades to a pale yellow while a snake plant leaf takes on a translucent yellow tone at the base. Matching up the symptoms to the plant species is a surefire way to tell if overwatering is the cause.

Match your houseplant to the symptoms and you have your diagnosis.

Large, thin-leafed tropical plants like monstera, calathea, anthurium and clumping philodendron typically show a bright yellow halo around a dark spot from overwatering. This happens because as roots begin to rot in soggy soil, fungal or bacterial pathogens in the potting mix travel up the plant and into the leaf tissue. Dead leaf cells show up as a black or brown area, and the bright ring of yellow around it is where the plant is attempting to stop the infection spreading.

ZZ plants (Zamioculcas zamiifolia), caladiums, and elephant ears (Alocasia and Colocasia) grow from potato-like rhizomes or tubers that store lots of water, so it can take these plants a little longer to show signs of overwatering. When they do, it's dramatic though! If these houseplants receive more water than they can process and rot sets in, nutrients are suddenly cut to a whole stem. The entire stalk and its foliage will quickly drain of color to turn a solid strong yellow, top to bottom.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Prayer plants (Maranta), peperomia, Chinese money plants (Pilea peperomioides), African violets (Saintpaulia), nerve plants (Fittonia) and Boston and maidenhair ferns all have a shallow network of very fine, fragile roots. Suffocating in overwatered soil, these thin roots quickly disintegrate and the leaves lose their lustre then become limp and fade through pale green to a matte yellow. Don’t expect these leaves to be mushy from all that water: because the root damage cuts the water supply off, leaves will become dry and brittle, snapping off immediately when touched or simply dropping from the plant.

Jade plants (Crassula ovata), snake plants, Christmas or Thanksgiving cacti (Schlumbergera), echeverias and aloe vera all store water in their stems or leaves, and excess moisture causes them to turn a translucent, sickly yellow at the base. The area will also feel mushy and this may happen where stems or leaves meet the soil, in which case stems may topple over, but also where leaves attach to stems or leaf segments join together.

Vining plants like pothos (Epipremnum aureum), English ivy (Hedera helix), wax plants (Hoya) and heartleaf philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) typically show overwatering symptoms on their oldest leaves near the base first. Unable to draw as many nutrients through suffocating roots, the plant strips nutrients from its older, less productive leaves to feed the fresh growth at its tips in the hope of finding a more suitable environment. Stripped of chlorophyll, the base foliage turns an even, uniform yellow while the newer growth at the stem tip remains green.

Overwatered houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants (Chlorophytum comosum) and ponytail palms (Beaucarnea recurvata) typically develop brown foliage tips with a yellow area separating them from the healthy green tissue. This happens because the leaf tips are at the very end of the plant's plumbing system so, when roots are damaged and can't take up water effectively, are the first to run out of moisture. The yellow color below the dead brown leaf tissue is the plant trying to salvage what nutrients it can. The leaves may lose their upright arch and start to droop, too.

If you spot yellowing houseplant leaves, immediately stop watering and let the soil dry out. Slide the pot off and if you see white roots, you’ve caught the problem in time. Pop the plant back into its pot and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry. A moisture meter like this from Amazon takes out the guesswork and helps you adjust your routine to the plant's fluctuating needs going forwards, and water houseplants properly.

If there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, and roots look dark, root rot has set in and you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp scissors or pruners or to snip off all roots that look dark or feel mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your houseplant.

It's vital the pot has a drainage hole so excess moisture can escape (and a saucer to save your surfaces). If you adore a decorative hole-less pot, use it as a cachepot with a holed plastic pot inside. For succulent plants that store water in their leaves or stems, fill your pot with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot. For everything else, use an indoor potting mix with coconut coir and perlite that evens out moisture levels while allowing good drainage like Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix For All Plants, available from Walmart.

Upgrade your irrigation with a watering can that has a long, gooseneck spout like this indoor can from Walmart for more precise, controlled water delivery.

#7804. Small, Inexpensive Projects That Will Transform Your Bathroom

Transforming your bathroom doesn’t have to require a massive budget or a total demolition and new layout to achieve a high-end feel. In fact, the National Kitchen & Bath Association 2026 Bath Trends Report notes that 64 percent of designers identify homeowners opting for smaller refreshes over large-scale renovations as a major emerging trend. By focusing on high-impact, affordable updates, you can revitalize your bathroom in a single weekend. This guide covers five simple, small bathroom projects that deliver professional results in no time.

Decluttering and finding effective storage solutions in your bathroom can not only make it look more appealing but will also create a more relaxing environment. It naturally feels far more refined and purposeful to have a more open surface, says Alan Solis, CEO of Solis Painting in Springfield, New Jersey. “By clearing countertops, taking unused products out of the equation, and reducing what is on display, you are instantly making it feel cleaner and more spacious,” explains Solis. Folding towels neatly and displaying them intentionally on a towel bar is another example of a small, free way to shift the mood of the room.

Choosing smart storage is another way to improve the look and feel of a bathroom. Paul McManus, president at McManus Kitchen and Bath in Tallahassee, Florida, recommends focusing on some simple organizers, such as vanity and medicine cabinet organizers. “Another easy way to add storage is to put a floating shelf or two over the toilet, especially in small bathrooms,” says McManus.

Another way to revamp a bathroom is to swap out existing hardware and fixtures—cabinet knobs and handles, towel bars, faucets, and the showerhead—with upgraded options. Modern finishes like brushed nickel or matte black are a quick way to create a more modern, polished look without having to invest in a larger project like replacing all the cabinetry, says Solis. Just be sure to keep the hardware consistent for a seamless look.

Replacing your showerhead is very easy and affordable; it boosts the look of the bathroom, saves water, and improves the experience of using your shower. McManus recommends choosing a dual-function showerhead, such as Delta’s In2ition line that features a detachable hand shower that can be used separately from or simultaneously with the showerhead.

The Keg towel warmer can be mounted to your wall or placed freestanding, and it holds two standard bath towels or a large robe. See our full review.

Upgrading the lighting in the space is a great value-minded way to improve a bathroom, says Craig Gritzen, founder and principal designer at Curated Style Collective in Salt Lake City, Utah.

“Consider upgrading light bulbs in your bathroom fixtures to switch-color white LED bulbs that toggle between daylight for grooming (6000K) and warm light for relaxing (3000k) to help promote a spa-like feel,” says Gritzen. If your budget allows, he also recommends upgrading lights from builder-grade to more design-forward fixtures that are damp-rated to make the space feel more luxe. It’s also effective to layer in soft lighting to create a warm, soothing atmosphere, which can be accomplished by installing dimmable light bulbs, sconces, and small table lamps.

Painting is still one of the best value upgrades that homeowners can tackle in a weekend, says Gritzen. He suggests choosing soft, warm whites; muted greens and blues; or other grounding earth tones for the walls to make a stark space feel more relaxing and spa-like. In addition, Solis recommends adding a fresh coat of paint to the vanity or cabinets. “Since bathrooms are smaller, this project is a fairly easy one with large visual impact,” notes Solis. If you’re not up for painting the entire bathroom, try simply cleaning up paint lines to help make the room feel noticeably fresher.

Another way to transform the vibe of a bathroom is to incorporate spalike elements that provide comfortable textures and refreshing fragrances. “New plush towels with matching tones, along with a bathmat and shower curtain, can have a large impact on the space,” notes Gritzen. Another way to increase the spa feel without breaking the bank is to install a few robe hooks to hang terrycloth robes.

Scent can also help a bathroom feel more Zen, says Gritzen. “Scent stimulates our olfactory system, which can be used strategically to promote relaxation,” explains Gritzen. He suggests setting up a diffuser with lavender, eucalyptus, or sandalwood essential oils to help promote relaxation.
