#7790. I Tested Anker’s New SOLIX S5000, and It Ran My Fridge for Days

Published Oct 28, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Living in Florida, where severe storms and power outages are always a possibility, I’ve tested quite a few portable power stations over the years. The new Anker Solix S5000 is one of the most impressive yet. With a massive 5,024-watt-hour (Wh) battery, 4,500 watts of output, and the ability to power both 120-volt and 240-volt appliances, it’s designed to keep your household essentials running when the grid goes down. After a month of testing it at my Florida home ahead of its October 27 release, I was particularly impressed by just how long it lasted.

Bottom line: The Anker Solix S5000 is a robust power solution for extended outages, offering impressive performance and versatility at a competitive price.

To see what the S5000 could realistically do during a blackout, I connected my refrigerator and let it run under normal operating conditions until the battery was depleted. Incredibly, it lasted around 86 hours, matching Anker’s advertised runtime. That’s more than 3.5 days of refrigeration without any additional charging, which could make an enormous difference during a prolonged outage. Of course, runtime will depend on your refrigerator’s energy consumption, but this was one of the most impressive results I’ve seen from a portable power station.

I also tested the S5000 with my portable air conditioner, lamps, chargers, and other household essentials, including running multiple appliances simultaneously. It handled everything I threw at it during normal use. The unit was virtually silent while powering my AC, though the internal cooling fans kicked in with a noticeable hum when I increased the electrical load.

I also tested its uninterruptible power supply (UPS) function by connecting my computer and disconnecting the S5000 from wall power. My PC continued running without even a flicker. Recharging the battery from empty to full took approximately 3.5 hours using a standard 120-volt household outlet. Anker claims a faster 99-minute recharge, though that requires a 240-volt connection, which I didn’t have available to test.

Despite its enormous capacity, the S5000 has a relatively small footprint, and its sturdy housing feels exceptionally well built. At 97 pounds, though, it’s certainly not lightweight. The built-in wheels and telescoping handle make it pretty easy to move across hard, flat floors. I even managed to maneuver it across my lawn, although the weight made uneven ground noticeably more challenging. Stairs are another story entirely, and you’ll almost certainly want a second person to help lift it.

My one minor design gripe is the telescoping handle, which feels more like something you’d find on a standard suitcase than a premium piece of power equipment. It works perfectly well, but I’ve tested other Anker equipment with more substantial handles.

At a regular price of $3,599.99, the Anker S5000 is a significant investment, though its introductory $2,499.99 price makes it a lot more appealing. If you’re looking to keep refrigerators, cooling equipment, lights, and other essentials running through an extended blackout, I think it’s an excellent option. The fact that you can expand its storage capacity up to 30kWh makes it even more versatile for future backup needs.

If you can live with its substantial weight, the Anker Solix S5000 gives you the kind of runtime and performance that makes it super useful when the power goes out.

#7788. 14 Secret Storage Spots for Hiding Valuables in Your Home

Updated Oct 28, 2026 11:22 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

According to the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer, 505,554 burglaries were reported in the U.S. between October 2025 and October 2026. Given the risk of theft, we often tuck our valuables—passports, jewelry, cash, important documents—in a bedside drawer, or maybe even in a small safe. But thieves know to rifle through drawers, and while safes afford some protection, they can be easy for burglars to spot, and it’s possible to break into them, whether they’re password-protected or key-operated. Knowing this, thieves may simply grab a safe and figure out later how to open it.

Outsmarting burglars by concealing your valuables in these unusual places might be the way to go to keep your things in your possession.

Keeping important items and documents secure inside a water- and fire-resistant safe is a good idea, but small home safes are primary targets for savvy thieves. Even worse, they are often portable enough to be picked up and carried off, which is a good argument for bolting a safe to the floor or a fixed shelf. To help protect valuables from thieves without sacrificing the fire resistance a home safe can provide, consider storing valuables inside the safe and concealing the safe itself inside empty luggage.

Certain valuables, like a physical will or a rainy day fund, may go untouched for weeks, months, or even years, so consider an out-of-the-way place to store these important possessions. One such spot is the space above the kitchen cabinets. In some kitchens, ½-inch gaps between the ceiling and the tops of upper cabinets, easily visible only from a ladder, offer a stealthy place.

First, fill a manila envelope with your valuables. Next, secure the envelope with a pair of broad binder clips to prevent it from sliding all the way into the gap, or fasten a string to the envelope for easy retrieval when necessary. Finally, slide the envelope into the gap.

Hiding valuables in a drawer isn’t likely to protect them against a determined thief. Instead, take advantage of the gap behind a drawer by using tape to secure an envelope filled with important documents, cash, or other valuables to the back of the drawer.

If the drawer pulls out too easily, threatening to expose the concealed envelope, attach the envelope to the underside of the counter, dresser, or bedside table so that even with the drawers fully removed the envelope will remain securely fastened to the furniture and out of sight.

Hanging picture frames, paintings, mirrors, and other wall decor throughout the house offer another opportunity to hide valuables. With a bit of tape and an envelope, any wall hanging can discreetly store important valuables.

While almost any framed wall hanging can help conceal items, a deep wooden frame offers a greater potential for subterfuge. If the frame is deep enough, you can neatly cut the paper backing and slide cash or prized possessions into the narrow gap between the artwork and the frame backing. Very thin items may even fit between a picture and the backing. To find the stashed valuables, would-be thieves would have to choose the right piece of artwork and remove the dust cover on the back of the frame—not easy to do quickly.

Creating secret storage spots out of common household items is a time-honored strategy. If you have a few shelves of books inside your home, consider hollowing a book out to make a small storage compartment inside the pages, making sure that the resulting “safe” looks unremarkable unless it’s removed from the shelf and opened.

An empty can is yet another easy secret storage spot, and one you can DIY. Using a smooth-edge can opener, open the can carefully so the top will fit neatly back into place. Empty the can out and clean it thoroughly. When it’s dry, fill it with valuables, replace the top, and return the can to a pantry or cabinet where it will blend in with the rest of your provisions. You can also purchase can safes festooned with realistic labels for corn, beets, tomatoes, and more.

The Jssmst book safe blends in easily on your bookshelf and is ideal for hiding small items like jewelry and passports. See our full review.

When burglars break into a home in search of valuables, they may not be able to take the time to tear through coats, sweaters, and other clothing hanging in the closet. Consider keeping an envelope of valuables in the pocket of an old jacket. You may want to switch the hiding spot when the seasons change, storing important possessions in winter clothing during the summer and summer clothing in the winter. If you have clothing with hidden pockets that can help conceal valuables, all the better.

Frozen pizzas, leftovers, and ice cream novelties keep many freezers tightly packed and conveniently crowded. One more container in the freezer probably won’t draw the attention of would-be thieves, making it a great place to stow cash and other valuables. Just make sure that both the container and the contents are freezer-safe to prevent damaging your important items.

As with an old book or an empty can, a tennis ball or soccer ball can be modified to create a secret storage spot. Tennis balls retain their shape after being cut, so they don’t look out of the ordinary with a slit halfway through the ball. As long as the opening is wide enough, it should be able to accommodate a roll of cash or small valuables like earrings or a ring.

For larger items, however, consider using a soccer ball. Just cut along one seam of the ball to create an opening that’s big enough to slide in your valuables. Cutting along the seam conceals the opening so the casual observer won’t be likely to notice anything odd about the ball.

A drop ceiling, a common feature in finished basements, laundry rooms, and utility rooms,  consists of panels or tiles that are supported by narrow metal frames. The hollow space above the panels can serve as a concealed storage location for lightweight items of value. Simply lift a panel to access the hollow space above and slide in a small packet, such as an envelope, a bag, or even a small box, to keep it out of sight.

This isn’t a spot for heavy items, which could break through the ceiling tile and fall to the ground below. Also, note which tile you’ve stashed the items behind so you can retrieve them easily later.

It isn’t a good idea to store valuable items in an actual air vent because you can block the flow of air into the home, reducing the efficiency of the heating and cooling system. Instead, consider installing a false air vent over an opening in the wall, specifically to store your valuables. Not many thieves are going to take the time to unscrew and check the air vents throughout the home.

Clocks are an excellent option for storing small, valuable items. Most mantel or wall clocks have open cavities in the back or base, where a few small items can be kept safe. If your clock doesn’t have an open cavity, simply tape valuables to the back of the clock and return it to the wall. As long as the clock itself isn’t worth stealing, your items should be safe in a break-in.

Another possibility is to store your valuables in a pillow or a couch cushion. Tuck flat valuables inside zippered cushion covers, and if your pillows don’t have zippers, just cut an opening in the back and stitch in a zipper (or even a hook-and-loop fastener). Take out some stuffing, insert the valuables, and close up the pillow. (Choose a pillow that is not frequently used, lest a visiting great-aunt stumble upon stacks of cash.)

Instead of throwing out your old canister-style vacuum cleaner when you upgrade to a new model, consider using it as a storage space for your valuables. After cleaning the inside of the canister thoroughly, hide your valuables inside. Store the old vacuum in the basement or closet along with your other cleaning supplies so it doesn’t attract attention or look out of place.

Any window seat or banquette that opens for storage offers a good place to cache your valuables, which you can toss in there with random blankets, board games, or tablecloths. If your window seat doesn’t open, consider transforming it into a storage bench—an accessible project for a handy homeowner. While you’re at it, try another clever DIY for stealthy storage: retrofitting drawers into existing stair treads.

#7786. The Fall Yard Reset: What to Cut, Plant, Mulch, and Leave Alone

Published Oct 28, 2026 11:57 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As the crisp autumn air moves in and summer perennials begin to fade, transitioning your outdoor space with a thoughtful approach to fall landscaping is the secret to a healthy, vibrant yard next spring. Cooler temperatures might signal that it is time to wind down yard work, but this is actually a critical season for maintenance, offering the ideal conditions for root establishment and garden prep.

Knowing exactly what to do can feel overwhelming, since various plants require entirely different approaches. We spoke to several landscaping experts to find out what kind of care each type of plant needs during this time of year.

Pruning plants can encourage new growth and fruit or flower production, shape a plant, or thin it out for better light and air circulation. Fall is a good time to cut back some perennials that have finished flowering, such as daylilies, hostas, and peonies, especially once their foliage starts dying back, says James de Lacey, owner of Texas Tree Post in Austin, Texas. “You can also remove dead, damaged, or diseased branches from trees and shrubs.” After a damaging frost, homeowners can cut back ornamental grasses to make way for new spring growth as well, adds Judd Fitzgerald, sales manager at Richlawn Company in Platteville, Colorado.

However, de Lacy recommends avoiding heavy pruning of most woody plants in the fall, particularly spring-flowering shrubs like lilacs, azaleas, forsythias, and rhododendrons because you risk cutting off next year’s flower buds.

BobVila.com’s product testers say these pruners perform best in terms of comfort, strength, durability, and ease of use.

Fall is one of the best times to plant deciduous trees like maples, oaks, and birches, along with shrubs, says de Lacey. Conifer ornamental trees are also good candidates for fall planting, adds Fitzgerald. As long as the ground isn’t frozen, plants and trees can keep growing roots through winter. Additionally, the cooler temperatures and naturally moist soil help roots establish without the stress of summer heat.

Fall is also an ideal time to plant spring-flowering bulbs like tulips, daffodils, alliums, and crocuses so they can go through the cold period they need to flower properly, says Jose Lopez, owner and founder of Williams Landscaping Inc. in Chicago, Illinois. “Hardy perennials like coneflowers and black-eyed Susans can also be planted in early fall, provided they have enough time to establish before the ground freezes,” notes de Lacy. However, avoid planting tender annuals or plants that need a long stretch of warm weather to establish when frosts are approaching, warns Lopez.

Anything you planted this year, including trees, shrubs, and perennials, can benefit from mulch for winter protection since the plants’ roots haven’t had much time to establish yet, says Lopez. “A couple inches of mulch on top of the soil can help protect the roots, but keep it pulled back from the trunk and stems,” he advises. “Think of mulch as a blanket, not a mound,” says Lopez. “If you pile it against the bark, it holds moisture and can contribute to rot. That’s the kind of problem we see when spring cleanup comes around.”

Roses and perennials with shallow roots can also need extra insulation, depending on the variety and how exposed the planting area is. Garlic planted in the fall also can benefit from a layer of mulch. If you have containers that need to stay outside, you’ll want to protect the roots inside because the soil in a container can freeze more quickly than the ground, says Lopez.

Some plants in fall landscaping don’t need any attention at all this time of year. You don’t need to prune established, climate-appropriate healthy trees and mature shrubs just because winter is coming. Plus, if there’s already enough mulch around them, there’s no need to add more, says Lopez. Mature maples, oaks, and other hardy deciduous trees can generally be left alone as they enter dormancy, adds de Lacey. Other plants to leave alone include:

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7781. Frost Coming Your Way? What to Do With Veggies in the Garden

Updated Oct 28, 2026 4:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

While some people welcome the cooling that accompanies autumn, gardeners know they have work to do before the coming frost kills off the literal fruits (and veggies) of their labor.

First, find out the typical frost dates for your USDA hardiness zone and learn what temperatures cause frost damage. Then, watch local weather forecasts. Understand the difference between frost and light freeze, and which plants are more susceptible to frost damage.

Start with healthy plants and the right soil. Next, you’ll need to know which plants are tender and which can withstand a light frost and which delicious homegrown fruits and vegetables you’ll need to harvest before it’s too late.

Tender plants are easily damaged by frost or cold weather, requiring protection to survive. Common tender fruits and vegetables include watermelon, squash, pumpkin, cantaloupe and muskmelon, eggplant, cucumber, okra, pepper, beans, tomatoes, and most herbs.

Frost-tolerant plants can withstand brief periods of cold or frost, but beyond very limited periods, would require protection. Examples of frost-tolerant plants include lettuce, cauliflower, endive, peas, carrots, Chinese cabbage, celery, chard, and chicory.

Hardy plants generally have higher levels of sugar in their leaves, which enables them to tolerate lower temperatures. Cool-season crops that can survive a frost or even an early freeze include asparagus, cabbage, kale, spinach, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, collards, potatoes, and onions.

Many crops can be saved from an early frost. Even cool-season crops like lettuce and other leafy greens, carrots, and radishes can benefit from overnight covering to protect the plants from frost and extend the growing season. You can use old sheets or drop cloths (using supports to keep the cover from touching the plants), burlap, row covers made of non-woven polyester, or cloches.

Whichever type of plant cover you choose, make sure it is breathable. Do not use plastic. Ensure air circulation and be sure to remove the covers during the heat of the day, and put them back on in the early evening.If you have a greenhouse, move as many plants as you can inside.

Bio Green’s heater has a digital thermostat, sturdy stainless steel build, and is intended for spaces up to 130 square feet. Read the review.

Adding a 2- to 4-inch layer of mulch, particularly in the afternoon while the soil is warm, can help protect roots from overnight dips in temperature. Material choices to minimize frost damage include wood chips, bark, pine needles, straw, and even shredded leaves (including if they’re moldy). Dark mulch absorbs more of the sun’s warmth, which it releases into the soil around the plants at night.

Mulching the garden also preserves much-needed moisture. In addition, a layer of mulch will prevent perennials from putting out new growth at the end of the season, allowing them to go dormant for the winter.

Moist soil actually holds up to four times more heat than dry soil, and conducts that heat to the soil surface faster, creating a microclimate in which the air above it is 5 degrees warmer. In addition to providing an insulating effect, water helps plants withstand temperature changes better.

For best results, water late in the day because the water vapor creates a microclimate that will help plants stay warm and resist freezing.

When all else fails, harvest what you can. Beans, peas, corn, melons, cucumbers, eggplant, and most greens should be harvested early, since they don’t handle frost well. Be sure to pick tender herbs such as basil and oregano.

Tomatoes and peppers can ripen indoors after harvest. In fact, many fruits, including apples, peaches, pears, grapes, cantaloupe, and persimmon, ripen after picking. Store pumpkins and squash in a dry location for later use.

It can be tough to eat all of the last harvest right away, but there are plenty of ways to preserve your bounty: dry herbs, and can, dry, or freeze fruits and vegetables.

Many fruits can ripen indoors more quickly if they’re kept in a paper bag that is loosely closed at the top. Storing them this way traps ethylene gas that helps ripen fruit. Because rice also traps ethylene gas, fruits can be placed in containers of rice, although this is not recommended for tender fruits such as peaches that can suffer bruising. Taking these steps can typically help fruit ripen within a few days.

Plastic bags are not advised for ripening fruit because they don’t allow for ventilation.

Not all produce has to be harvested at the first sign of frost. Many root vegetables, like beets, carrots, onions, turnips, parsnips, and potatoes can easily survive a light frost. So can kale, artichokes, broccoli, cabbage, radishes, leeks, spinach, Brussels sprouts, and chard. In fact, cold temperatures improve the flavor of crops such as carrots and kale.

Several of these can even survive a hard frost, including broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, collards, kale, kohlrabi, mustard, onions, parsley, peas, radishes, spinach, turnips, leeks, and sorrel.

If frost gets your fruits and vegetables, they may not be edible. Tender plants like peppers, tomatoes, and many fruits may be mushy. Lettuces and other greens often turn dark and limp. Beans, eggplant, and potatoes are also susceptible to frost, and may exhibit crystalized moisture in their cells. Even carrots can become rubbery or limp after a hard frost.

If the produce is past its prime, dispose of it in your compost pile or bin, where it can benefit next year’s garden.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7779. How to Wrap a Tree to Protect it From Winter Damage

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

It may sound like an odd practice, but wrapping a tree can be worthwhile. Once trees drop their leaves, they no longer benefit from their protective canopy, and hazards can damage young and thin-barked trees, along with some evergreen trees and shrubs. “Cold temperatures, drying winds, ice, and hungry wildlife can injure trees during winter,” says Fred Breglia, ISA, a certified arborist and author of the upcoming book titled Big Trees: A Tour of the World’s Biggest Trees.

And it’s not just the cold that makes trees susceptible to damage. Adding a tree wrap around the trunk can protect the bark from harsh winter sun when leaves no longer shade it. Ahead, learn why tree wrapping helps some trees flourish and survive colds—and how you can wrap trees for winter safely and effectively.

Young trees, like those that have been growing for up to two seasons, are especially susceptible to winter damage. Wrapping immature and thin-barked trees helps prevent trunk damage from sun and freeze-thaw cycles. Some evergreens also benefit from a full-tree wrap for winter or a screen to prevent browning foliage, and other young trees can be saved from animal munching or rubbing damage with a fence wrap.

Rapid temperature changes in winter combine with an empty canopy to expose trees to frost cracks or sunscald. Vertical frost cracks can make a tree more vulnerable to pests or diseases.  Sunscald is even more serious. “Sunlight warms frozen bark, then shade or nightfall causes it to refreeze and die,” says Breglia. Sunscald usually occurs on a trunk’s southwest side, where winter sun is most intense and the bark warms up the most. It can cause a jagged vertical wound along the tree trunk and dry, cracked, sunken, or dead bark.

Trees are more susceptible to sunscald include those less than 2 years old and species with thin bark, such as:

Another type of cold damage is winter browning, or desiccation injury, which “occurs when evergreen needles and rhododendron leaves lose moisture faster than frozen soil can replace it,” says Breglia. He adds that low temperatures, freeze-thaw cycles, sun, and wind can worsen winter damage on evergreens or semi-evergreens. “Browning often occurs on the south or southwest side of conifers, though wind exposure may also damage the north side,” Breglia says.

Trees and shrubs most susceptible to winter browning include broadleaf evergreens, needled evergreens, or those with scale-like leaves, such as:

Deer and other browsers can munch on buds of trees in winter when food is scarce, but they also can bite into tender bark. Even in early fall, bucks look for small tree trunks to rub against as new antlers form and cause itching. “Voles, mice, and rabbits can severely damage young trees and shrubs by eating their bark in winter,” adds Breglia.

As always, young trees are most vulnerable to severe damage, along with some trees that wildlife prefer.

If you have a young tree or a tree or shrub species vulnerable to winter damage, you generally need to learn how to use tree wrap so you can prepare it in fall before the first winter frost. The precise timing varies by region and the type of damage that can occur. For example, if deer visit your landscape, you might need to wrap young trunks by late summer or as soon as you see bucks growing antlers.

For potential vole and mice damage, wrap trunks before the first snowfall. Most young trees will benefit from wrap protection for at least two winter seasons. In all cases, be sure to remove tree wraps by spring and never leave them on all year.

The most common way to wrap a tree trunk for winter tree protection is with a poly or fabric tree wrap or plastic guard. A tree wrap should be breathable and a light color. Breglia says the material should “conform to the trunk but also allow airflow without trapping moisture.”

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Using a small trowel or shovel, gently scrape away any debris or leaves against the trunk and dig about 1 inch below the soil surface all around the trunk. This helps to set your tree wrap taut against the trunk and just below ground level.

Start at the lowest point of trunk exposure and begin to wrap around the trunk, ensuring each pass overlaps by at least ⅓ of the wrap’s width so there is no exposed bark.

If you’re using a plastic guard, widen the opening and place it around the tree, ensuring it sits just below ground level.

Continue to wrap the trunk until you reach the area just below the tree’s lowest branch. When you’re finished wrapping, secure the wrap with heavy-duty tape or twine. Do not staple or puncture the tree.

If using a plastic guard, add another guard above the lower one, cutting it if necessary to end just below the branches. Secure it to the bottom guard per manufacturer directions or with heavy-duty tape.

Check the wrap from time to time to make sure it remains secure at the top and has not loosened or been damaged below.

When the cold weather is over, carefully remove the wrap from the tree.

Although you can loosely wrap an entire shrub or tree in burlap to prevent winter browning, it is best to build a barrier around the plant, typically with stakes. “Use a burlap windbreak placed a few inches from the foliage, or loosely wrap multistemmed evergreens to block drying winter winds without trapping moisture,” says Breglia. If you wrap a tree or shrub in the fabric to protect it from wind or moisture loss, leave a hole at the top to allow sun and air to get in.

If you want to prevent winter wind damage like browning, install a burlap or shade fabric screen around the tree. Here’s how:

As long as your tree wrap is secure and at least 1 inch below ground, it can protect the trunk from most small animal damage. If you only need to protect against animals and not sunscald or browning, consider this method suggested by Breglia:

When wrapping trees for winter, always remember to remove the tree wrap in spring. Each spring, check trees and shrubs for any damage as growth resumes, like discolored needles, split bark, or areas that appear to have been nibbled on or stripped by animals. Breglia also advises watering trees well in spring and summer (and after planting a tree) so they are healthy when entering the winter season.

When properly placed, tree wrap can protect many trees and shrubs from winter damage. The trunks of young and thin-barked trees are particularly vulnerable to frost cracks, sunscald, and animal damage, so covering the trunk can keep a tree from the type of damage that could eventually result in taking the tree down and replanting.

Tree trunks are best wrapped in light-colored breathable fabrics especially designed for tree wrapping or plastic tree guards that surround a trunk. Some gardeners use burlap, but it can result in damage and is best used as a light wrap or screen to protect trees from winter browning or animal damage. Breglia recommends against the use of wound paint or dressing for young trees; paint will not protect trees from animal damage.

Always wait to wrap a tree in fall as it goes dormant and before the first hard frost. If you miss the first frost, wrap the tree as soon as the trunk has dried out to prevent repeated injury. Never wrap or leave wrap on a tree in spring or summer growth phases. And the best time to wrap a tree is when it is young (first 1 to 3 years of growth).

Some trees or shrubs need only temporary winter protection from unusual frosts or storms. A burlap screen or windbreak also can protect trees in winter. Spreading a 2- to 3-inch layer of mulch around the tree, at least the width of its root ball or canopy, can protect tender roots from repeated winter freezing and thawing. Breglia says that anti-dessicant sprays can help prevent drying out of trees and shrubs. Fencing can keep browsing animals away from evergreens.  “Proper placement of winter injury-sensitive plants, such as rhododendrons, boxwood, yew, or arborvitae can reduce the chance of winter damage,” adds Breglia. Finally, healthy trees can best survive winter, so watering and other care steps in spring and summer help protect tender trees in winter.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

Stepping into a chilly bathroom isn’t the most pleasant experience, but fortunately, there is a wide range of bathroom heaters that can quickly warm any bathroom. Dreo’s wall-mount space heater took top honors for its quick heating, safety features, and its ability to be controlled remotely.

In addition to the units we tested, several others met our high standards for quality, safety, and innovation, and we’ve included them here as well. Keep reading to learn more about how the following models earned their spots on our lineup of the best bathroom heaters.

Bottom line: Discover the best bathroom heaters of 2026, from top-performing wall-mounts to budget-friendly options, ensuring a warm and comfortable space.

We tested the first four bathroom heaters on this list, and you’ll find a variety of options suited for various types of bathroom layouts and budgets. From wall-mount models that don’t take up floor space to small personal options for dressing nooks, these are some of the best bathroom heaters for keeping your space comfy.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Functionality 4.8/5; Noise 4.8/5; Value 4.8/5

Dreo has a winner with the Dreo WH517S smart space heater. We liked being able to hang this space heater on the wall, where it was up and out of the way, rather than sitting on a wet bathroom floor. Installation was simple: Dreo included a mounting template that indicated the location for the screws, and best of all, the template came with a bubble level so that we could ensure the heater would be perfectly straight.

Setting up the app was a snap. All we had to do was plug the Dreo WH517S into the wall socket and turn it on. We already had the Dreo app on our smartphone, which immediately recognized the heater. If you don’t have the app, a QR code walks you through the steps.

We tested the space heater in a small, 65-square-foot bathroom located at the end of an HVAC duct run, so it always felt cold during the winter—until now. On a day when the outdoor temperatures were in the single digits, the WH517S raised the bathroom’s temperature from a chilly 58 degrees to 70 degrees in about 20 minutes.

This heater also comes with an ALCI plug option capable of shutting the heater off when it senses abnormal electric flow. It also has an IP24 rating, so it can take an occasional splash of water. In homes with small children, this heater can be mounted high on the wall for added safety.

What our tester says: “On winter mornings, I love being able to turn on the heater in the bathroom from my smartphone without having to get out of bed. Just 15 minutes and the bathroom is warm and comfortable for my shower.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Dreo Wall-Mount bathroom heater at Amazon or Dreo.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4.5/5; Functionality 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Value 4.3/5

You don’t have to spend a lot to warm up a chilly bathroom. The Lasko 1500W bathroom space heater is compact, comes with an ALCI safety plug, and best of all, is affordable.

This Lasko heater doesn’t have many bells and whistles, but it’s a solid pick to heat a small- to medium-size bathroom. It measures just 8 inches tall by 6.25 inches wide and weighs just 3.35 pounds, making it small enough to sit on a bathroom shelf or countertop.

In our tests, this budget-friendly heater raised the temperature of our bathroom by 10 degrees in under 30 minutes when we ran it on high. We liked the option of choosing high or low power, and the heater’s 1-hour setting ensures it won’t continue to produce heat after an hour if someone leaves it running.

It comes with a cool-touch case that didn’t get hot after an hour of running the heater on high, but the grille on the front of the heater did get hot, so we’d suggest locating this bathroom heater out of the reach of pets and little hands.

Get the Lasko 1500W bathroom heater at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Performance 5/5; Functionality 5/5; Noise 5/5; Value 4.5/5

Thanks to its quiet operation, effective heating, and feature-rich design, this slim and stylish Dreo heater earned nearly perfect marks in all our tests. Though it weighs under 5 pounds and isn’t even 6 inches in diameter, it had no difficulty warming spaces significantly larger than its 200-square-foot recommended area. For that reason, we especially appreciate that it comes with a remote with an impressive 26-foot range, as we regularly have to turn it off during our baths in order to keep ourselves from getting too warm.

Still, remotes are fairly commonplace for these types of appliances, so Dreo upped the ante by adding 70-degree oscillation, a 12-hour timer, a programmable thermostat, three heat settings, and fan-only operation. The heater also features an ALCI plug, V-0 flame-retardant construction, overheating and tip-over protection, and an inline carry handle. While it did take us a bit of fumbling to figure out this unit’s touch-control buttons at first, it wasn’t so complicated that we needed to consult the manual, and we’ve now used it without issue almost every day for nearly 2 months.

Get the Dreo Solaris bathroom heater at Amazon or Dreo.

The following bathroom heaters were not personally tested, but we chose them for our lineup based on their quality, features, and consumer ratings. If you’re still looking for the right model, you’ll likely find it here.

A ceiling-mounted bathroom heater doesn’t use up valuable floor or wall space, and when properly installed, there should be no safety issues. The Panasonic WhisperWarm goes one better by integrating a bathroom vent with a heater in a single low-profile unit.

We like the exhaust fan, which can be set to run at 50, 80, or 110 cubic feet per minute (CFM) to suit a variety of room sizes. The heater has a fixed output of 1600W but can be connected to a thermostat, allowing full control over room warmth. The Panasonic WhisperWarm uses the brand’s own intelligent DC motor, making it an energy-efficient space heater. The grille can be adjusted to direct warm air.

A Flex-Z fast bracket is designed to simplify installation, and the Panasonic can be fitted to either 4-inch or 6-inch ducting. A dimmable LED is also an option (though at extra cost). If a ceiling-mount heater isn’t already installed, we suggest hiring an electrician, because this unit requires a dedicated electric circuit.

Get the Panasonic bathroom heater at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

The main draw of a bathroom heater with a fan is to spread the heat as rapidly as possible around the room, but a downside can be extra noise. The Stiebel Eltron wall heater is different in that it delivers warmth quickly while running at just 49 decibels, which is about the level of a modern refrigerator.

Its maximum output is 1500W, which Stiebel Eltron rates as sufficient for rooms up to 150 square feet. A built-in thermostat regulates performance, and we like its 60-minute boost timer, with the unit automatically reverting to its previous setting at the end of the period. There is also a frost protection setting and an on/off switch that shuts down the whole unit to prevent accidental use.

Keep in mind that this is a hardwired unit, so it can’t simply plug into an outlet. If there’s no existing hardwired heater, professional installation is a good idea.

Get the Stiebel Eltron bathroom heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Wall heaters for bathrooms can save valuable floor space, but they can also butt into the room, providing a frustrating obstacle. The Broan-NuTone Comfort-Flo is a recessed or in-wall bathroom heater that provides a low-profile solution that we love for small bathrooms where space is at a premium. The louvers direct the heat flow downwards, helping to spread warmth evenly, and a front-mounted knob controls the built-in thermostat.

The Broan-NuTone Comfort-Flo is factory-wired at 1500W and 120 volts. It can be converted to 750W at 120 volts or 1500W at 240 volts, which may suit some installations. Note that the choice of watts is final; it does not offer two output levels. Installation is fairly straightforward, but we suggest hiring an electrician if this heater isn’t replacing an existing bathroom with a dedicated circuit.

Get the Broan-NuTone bathroom heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

When we started researching modern bathroom heating options, we quickly discovered that there were hundreds of different models available. After carefully considering nearly 50 choices, we settled on eight top models, and then we chose four of those to test in our own bathrooms.

We also looked at how safe the various models were for use in standard bathrooms. Remodeling expert Benjamin Stenson, director of operations of Norsemen, a home remodeling contractor in Louisville, Kentucky, told us, “Safety features are paramount, so users must opt for heaters designed to withstand bathroom conditions.”

Hands-on testing consisted of assessing the quality of each heater’s build, trying out each of its features, and keeping records of how quickly each one heated a small bathroom during cold weather. We noted how hot the exterior of the heaters became after an hour of continuous use, and we awarded points based on a rubric—the better a bathroom heater performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we summed the points and used them to determine our best overall pick and assign relevant categories for the others.

While the appearance of a bathroom heater will always impact choice, there are a number of technical aspects to consider. The information below will help shoppers choose the most appropriate types of electric bathroom heaters for their needs.

The three general types of heaters for bathrooms include portable bathroom heaters, wall-mounted heaters, and ceiling-mounted heaters. Most (but not all) space heaters for bathroom use are electric. It’s harder to find non-electric heaters than electric heaters for bathroom use.

The term “portable” can refer to various bathroom heaters, including plug-ins, space heaters, and oil-filled radiators. These are usually among the most affordable bathroom heaters. Their distinguishing design feature is that they are not permanently fitted to the bathroom wall or ceiling, so they can be used in other rooms. Some are very light and easy to move. Space heaters often have carry handles. Although oil-filled radiators are heavier, they can still be moved if necessary. All of these might be good options for bathrooms not in regular use, such as in a guest accommodation.

The main advantage of wall-mounted bathroom heaters is that they don’t take up valuable floor space. They can also be very discreet. Wall-mounted exhaust fans are sometimes combined with heater elements, though these generally have more modest output.

Much like wall-mounted models, a ceiling-mounted bathroom heater can be both powerful and discreet. Its position also keeps it well away from small children and pets. Many are combined with an exhaust fan, which is a benefit but can complicate installation. Some ceiling models are infrared space heaters that use a large red bulb to radiate heat downward.

Physical size will have an impact on choice, especially in smaller bathrooms. Plug-ins and small bathroom heaters can be an effective option, though recessed wall units and ceiling models have no space penalty at all once installed.

Actual heat output can be difficult to assess on an electric heater. Most indoor room heaters are rated in watts. Opinions vary, but many experts quote 5 to 10 watts per square foot as optimal for comfortable warmth. However, manufacturer figures may contradict this rule of thumb and are perhaps a better guide. Models described as providing “supplemental” heat might also fall below this standard, but it does depend on bathroom size. Bathroom heaters that provide thermostats or two output settings offer greater control over personal comfort.

Water and electricity are a dangerous mix, with a risk of serious electrical shock. The descriptive materials for any heater intended for use in the bathroom should clearly state that it is for bathroom use, but we could not find any official guidelines. Ceiling heaters for bathrooms present little risk when installed correctly because there are no exposed heater elements or plugs.

Other units may be at risk of water splashes, so thought should be given to positioning. In addition, there is some risk at wall outlets. The usual solution is to fit either an ALCI or GFCI safety plug. Both will cut power in a fraction of a second and prevent harm. Many manufacturers provide these, but they can also be retrofitted.

Some use portable propane heaters in bathrooms and other interior rooms, but if you choose that option, make sure the heater is designed for inside use. Some will give off dangerous fumes.

There’s a lot of detailed information in the article above, and we hope it answers most questions that often crop up regarding choosing the best bathroom heater. While doing our research, we came across some queries of a more general nature, and we have addressed those here.

The best way to heat a small bathroom is often with either a portable heater, a fan-less wall panel, or a heated towel rack for the bathroom. These provide sufficient heat but are either very quiet or completely silent.

Bathroom heaters are absolutely worth it, as anyone who has had to bathe in a cold bathroom will attest. What’s more, many are very affordable as well as economical to run, so users can have a little luxury without a big bill.

Many different types of heaters are allowed in bathrooms, ranging from low-cost portable models to a variety of wall- and ceiling-mounted options. Our collection of top bathroom heaters listed above underlines the wide choice available.

Bathroom heaters are perfectly safe to use when installed and operated following the manufacturer’s recommendations. Sometimes it’s as simple as having an ALCI safety plug fitted. With others, the wiring is hidden and out of harm’s way.

It’s not a good idea if it’s a continuously running heater. However, if you have a permanently installed heater that runs on a thermostat, it’s probably okay. For trips to the restroom at night, consider a heated toilet seat and leave the space heater off.

Use 10 watts per square foot of floor space as a guide when sizing any kind of heater. For example, a 1500W bathroom heater will warm a 150-square-foot bathroom efficiently.

If it’s hardwired, probably. If it’s a high-capacity heater (1500W or up) that plugs into an outlet, it could overload the circuit if several other appliances are plugged in at the same time.

#7773. Bonfire Season Is Here — Here Are the Dos and Don’ts for Staying Safe

How to not to expose yourself to toxic fumes, burn down the neighborhood and injure the kiddos, plus other tips for enjoying a stress-free bonfire.

Cool fall evenings naturally put our minds on the merits of bones-warming bonfires. And while many create cherished family memories and set the backdrop for festive community events, some end up in tragedy, with emergency room visits and property damage.

“Every season there are always the same preventable mistakes made that lead to injuries,” says attorney Kevin Henrichson. “Falling into the fire, using gasoline, adding fuel when you shouldn’t, failing to supervise children and consuming alcohol all raise the stakes of something bad happening.”

Ahead, experts walk through exactly what to do and not to do to stay safe while enjoying a bonfire.

Notify your local fire department of your plans and ask them for guidance concerning:

“One phone call to the fire marshal’s office takes two minutes,” says fire and home safety expert Eugene Klimaszewski. “Otherwise, the consequence of burning without a permit on a restricted day is a fine, and if it gets away from you, it’s your liability.”

Look for a flat, open spot away from fences, barns, houses, trees and ground vegetation. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) recommends keeping bonfires at least 25 feet from the house and other structures.

“That number isn’t arbitrary,” says Klimaszewski. “Radiant heat and drifting embers are what ignite a deck railing, a vinyl fence or the mulch bed against the house. Every ember that lands on a roof or in a gutter full of dry leaves is a coin flip. Most go out. The one that doesn’t becomes a structure fire.”

Build the fire downwind of your home and close all windows and doors on the fire side, to prevent smoke from getting in.

“Even a small amount of smoke reaching an indoor smoke detector is enough to set it off,” says Klimaszewski. If you have a monitoring system, that could trigger a call to the fire department. “At best that’s an embarrassing conversation with the engine company. In towns that charge for repeat false alarms, that’s a bill on top of the embarrassment,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you have an older home, which isn’t airtight, put your alarm system on test mode or notify your monitoring company about your bonfire plans.

Wind can carry embers up to a mile, which means a bonfire on a windy day can easily end with a wildfire or house fire. If your planned bonfire day turns out to be windy, reschedule it. And even if there isn’t a breeze, plan for one by clearing all debris from around the fire pit and building rocks or bricks up higher on the windy side, which protects the fire from the wind plus radiates heat toward you for extra warmth.

Kiln-dried wood is the best. Seasoned hardwoods like oak, cedar and hickory are particularly good because they burn cleaner, longer and hotter than soft woods like pine and aspen (though a little soft wood kindling makes starting a fire a lot easier).

Steer clear of gasoline or other accelerants, as they too often lead to burn injuries, out-of-control fires and noxious fumes. (One year, my neighbor used so much gasoline to start a bonfire that the resulting shock wave from the explosion knocked pictures off of people’s walls three blocks away).

“A lot of people think they can use gas or lighter fluid to get the fire started or revive it, but please never do that because the vapors can flash back and get everyone nearby,” says Henrichson. “Gasoline is particularly dangerous and should never be used to start or revive a fire.”

Pro-tip: If you struggling to start a fire, build up a good kindling base and use a campfire starter or small bit of tightly twisted newspaper. Ample kindling will help you get a hot coal-bed established, which will burn larger logs more effectively plus lessen smoke.

Avoid newspaper, cardboard and other paper products, which tend to break down into large flying embers. Also, never burn anything with adhesives, plastics and other chemicals. The health risks of this are obvious, but plastics and chemicals are hiding in many items you might not realize, including: dryer lint, food packaging with shiny ink, glossy magazines, pressed woods including butcher block, varnished furniture and clothing made with synthetic fibers.

Before lighting the fire, set up a water source in case embers become a problem. That will also make it easier to put it out completely when you’re done. NFPA actually requires a hose, bucket or extinguisher be on hand for all recreational fires, and for fires to be attended at all times.

“A fire that’s left alone for ten minutes while everyone goes inside for more drinks is the one that ends up on the local news,” says Klimaszewski. “And an unattended fire that spreads is the homeowner’s liability, full stop.”

Assign someone to supervise the flames at all times to prevent the fire from getting out of control, and to keep kids and pets from standing too close. Equip the supervisor with proper protective clothing, including a fire-resistant glove, long-handled poker tool, shovel, closed-toe shoes and eye protection.

“The most common injuries I’ve seen are from people falling into the fire, and young children are vulnerable to this because they may want to play in the area where everyone is hanging out by the fire,” says Henrichson. “There should be a no-enter zone that is explained to children every single time, and the person tending the fire should not have any alcohol.”

Watch for loose sleeves, blankets, boots and other combustibles that are too close to the fire. “Those fun marshmallow-roasting memories are great to make, but shaking a burning marshmallow can cause trouble, and if you use metal skewers, they can burn you too,” says Henrichson.

Also, know what to do beforehand if something ends up catching fire. “The old advice that we were told years ago is still true: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire,” says Henrichson. “Repeat this as necessary every time kids approach, because they don’t always know to stay back.”

Embers can easily reignite hours or even days later, so the best practice for putting out a bonfire is to drown it, stir the ashes, and then drown it again until everything is cold to the touch. Don’t cover embers with dirt, as that actually insulates them, leaving open the possibility for them to reignite if they’re uncovered by a stiff wind.

Pro-tip: Put ashes in a metal container with a lid, on a non-combustible surface, away from the house, garage and deck for several days before they go in the trash, says Klimaszewski. Never put them in a plastic bin or next to the house.

The following top picks feature both premium brands and budget alternatives as well as tool sets suited to indoor, outdoor, or interchangeable use. Read on to learn more about some of the best fireplace tools for any purpose.

When many options are available to suit individual preferences, this five-piece set from Amagabeli is appealing for its combination of desirable features and value for money. The tools are made from wrought iron, so they should last for many years. Featuring a classic style that’s smart, but not overly ornate, these fireplace tools can fit with a variety of decors.

The handles are comfortable and available in a black, brass, or gold-plated finish to match the other fireplace accessories. Tool reach is sufficient for large indoor fireplaces and outdoor pits. The support must be assembled, but that involves only tightening two nuts. Once together, the “gravity” base provides a sturdy platform.

Get the Amagabeli fireplace tools at Amazon.

Williams Sonoma is known for providing quality furniture and accessories, and this midcentury fireplace set is a fine example. Each piece looks finely crafted, and the corn stalk fiber broom shows particular attention to detail. The set is compact, but the curved support provides for easy access to each tool when needed.

These are fireplace tools that would look equally at home in front of a classic open fireplace grate, insert, or stove. Construction is steel throughout, finished in either matte black or burnished brass. The stand incorporates a tray so any ash that falls from the tools is contained. There are also rubber feet so it doesn’t slide around or mark flooring.

Get the Williams Sonoma fireplace tools at Williams Sonoma.

At the low end of the price scale, this log rack and tool set from Best Choice Products has a full set of tools, including tongs, yet it costs far less. While it looks less robust than some options, it’s reasonably well made. The rack requires a little more assembly than some, but it’s not difficult. If care is taken when putting it together, it will be sturdy enough for a weight rating of 150 pounds.

Both rack and the fireplace tools are described as wrought iron; however, many independent reviewers believe they are powder-coated steel. It’s still a durable material but not recommended for outdoor use.

A good ash bucket is an indispensable fireplace tool for cleaning the fireplace or removing excess ash for better burning. While any steel bucket could do the job, the high-capacity F2C ash bucket is custom designed for the job and offers several advantages.

Construction is from galvanized iron, a material that has good resistance to corrosion. There’s a lid that keeps the contents secure, and it greatly reduces the chances of accidentally dropping hot ashes on the floor or hearth rugs. The long reach of some fireplace tools means gloves aren’t always necessary, but it’s a good idea to have some handy for when it’s necessary to get close or while opening a hot fireplace insert or stove door. Those splitting their own logs into more manageable sizes or kindling want a good axe, and few can match the quality or performance of the Estwing Fireside Friend. This U.S.-made tool is forged from a single piece of steel, so it’s practically indestructible. It is also superbly balanced, making the 4-pound head easy to handle.

The handle is wrapped in a patented shock-reduction grip that absorbs up to 70 percent of the impact energy, dramatically reducing the chances of stress-related injuries.

Get the Estwing fireplace tool at Amazon.

When selecting the best fireplace tools, the challenge is finding the right blend of strength, durability, and style. What suits one person could be entirely inappropriate for another. In every case, manufacturing quality is the prime consideration, but caveats exist. Sometimes, high-value fireplace tools, while functional, may not have the strength of those manufactured by premium brands.

Nicole Cullum, interior designer and founder of the wallpaper and textile company Color Caravan based out of Taos, New Mexico, has helpful design advice when it comes to choosing fireplace tools: “Fireplace tools are most certainly an opportunity to blend function and design.” While they need to be long lasting, there is also the opportunity for “turning a basic tool into an artistic sculptural moment.”

Safety is also important. Fire Program Specialist Bruce D. Bouch, MPIO, of the U.S. Fire Administration says: “It is important to purchase quality tools that will not readily fail during use. Check the connections on the tools for stability and the quality of the stand if provided.” He also cautions that “ash collection should only be completed with a metal can with a tight-fitting lid designed for that purpose. Embers from a fire become insulated within the remaining ashes and can readily ignite combustible items.”

While every fireside tools set is designed to perform the same basic functions, a number of factors affect their suitability for a particular location, including decor style, size, material, number of tools included, and more. Below are details about key considerations shoppers often keep in mind while choosing the best fireplace tools.

While product photography can provide a detailed impression of the style of a particular fireplace tool set, it can be misleading in terms of size. For example, a set that looks heavy duty might actually be much shorter than depicted.

Always check the set’s physical dimensions. Tool length is not always provided, but knowing the overall height of the stand allows a reasonably accurate estimate. Width and depth of the set also can have an impact, depending on its intended location.

Fireplace tool sets usually include four pieces: a poker (or stoker), tongs, broom (or brush), and shovel (or pan), and the stand to complete what is typically called a five-piece set. Some sets omit the tongs.

Fireplace tools are usually made of brass, steel, stainless steel, or wrought iron.

Brass is decorative, but it has limited strength because brass sets were originally intended for coal fireplaces, not logs. Anyone installing a faux fireplace or gas fireplace might buy a brass set as decoration, but it’s not recommended for day-to-day use.

Wrought iron is more resistant to corrosion than brass and likely to be more durable, so it’s usually recommended for outdoor use. Wrought iron will rust eventually, and both plain steel and wrought-iron fireplace tools often have an additional coating for increased protection.

Stainless steel is highly resistant to rust but almost always more expensive. Considerable debate exists as to whether steel or wrought-iron tools are stronger. It depends on the steel composition and, with fireplace tools, that information usually isn’t available.

Consider how the shovel and broom are attached to their shafts as this also can impact durability. Shovels may be welded or riveted; the former is usually stronger. Brooms may have a replaceable head, but not always.

Traditional wrought-iron fireplace tools were naturally blackened or grayed during the forging process. Today, unless they’re handmade, the wrought-iron tools either will be painted or, more likely, have a tough powder-coated finish. The handles might be chromed or brass plated. While brass lacks strength on its own, as a coating, it is acceptable.

Style is very personal, and there are many designs to consider. Rope work is common, as are twists and scrolls. Other tools can be quite plain and minimalist. While decorative elements are always a key consideration, the functionality shouldn’t be overlooked. It’s particularly important that fireplace tools are easy to grip. If there’s an existing fireplace screen, consider tools that match that item.

Stability is also key. It’s almost inevitable that the fireplace tool stand will get bumped at some point. A flat base plate works well on a perfectly even floor but also check the material thickness. If it’s thin and lightweight, it might get knocked over easily. Those stands with four or five feet will probably balance better on surfaces that aren’t perfectly level.

When fireplace tools are purchased online, a modest amount of assembly may be required. The tool support stem may need to be attached to the base of the stand, for example. If a log basket is part of the set, it may need to be bolted together. Generally, a screwdriver and/or wrench is all that’s required.

#7768. I Thought I Wanted a Single-Family Home. Turns Out, I Missed the Rental Income

We thought we wanted a single-family home, but adding an ADU made it the perfect place for us.

I’ve always had benchmarks for knowing when I’ve “made it” in life: a car with power windows and locks, a refrigerator with a water dispenser and owning a single-family home. The last one stems from the fact that my wife and I always owned two-family homes. We lived in one unit and rented out the other for over a decade before we finally had the means to move into a single-family home.

But the funny thing was, when we finally got there, something was missing. Our single-family home didn’t feel as rewarding as I thought it would. Ahead, I share why this long-sought-after dream house didn’t quite feel like one and how a new Massachusetts law allowed us to add the missing piece to our family’s forever home.

After 10 years of renting, my wife and I wanted to buy a home. We decided on a two-family property because we were nervous about taking on too much financially. A single-family home seemed like a luxury that was out of reach, but the rental income from a two-family home made homeownership seem feasible and financially safe. Collecting that first rent check was an amazing feeling, and it cut our mortgage payment in half. We were hooked. Being landlords wasn’t always stress-free, but regular rental income gave us so much financial freedom.

Seven years later, we moved into another two-family home that better suited our growing family and kept the first one, too. We continued to work and save for another five years. As we approached 40, buying a single-family home felt like the next logical step. It was the ultimate end goal, right? So we bought a single-family fixer-upper in a nice neighborhood and started making repairs. Our kids settled into a new school district, and we made friends with the neighbors.

At first, it all felt great, but living in a single-family home wasn’t everything we’d hoped it would be. Mostly, we found we really missed the rental income we were used to in our two-family homes. It felt foolish to have a house that only took money out of our bank account without putting any back in. We didn’t want to move, and soaring home prices made buying another property out of the question. To find ways to generate income from our property, I tried renting out our in-ground pool, second garage, and backyard to dog owners. None of those ideas panned out, leaving us without a way to recreate the two-family experience we missed.

Then, in August 2024, Massachusetts enacted a new law to encourage homeowners to build accessory dwelling units (ADUs), or in-law apartments, to ease the state’s housing shortage. These secondary, self-contained living spaces, complete with kitchens and bathrooms, can house extended family members or paying tenants.

My wife and I immediately knew this could be the solution we’d been looking for. Instead of moving to a two-family home, we could add a small apartment to our existing home. We considered our options and decided that converting a portion of our house into a one-bedroom apartment was the most cost-effective.

We researched town and state ordinances and building codes, then applied for a building permit and submitted plans for the proposed project. Because we weren’t changing the footprint of our home, the process went very smoothly. We started the work in August and had everything completed and inspected by December 2024. We received a certificate of occupancy from the town, and our first tenant moved in on January 1, 2025.

Nearly two years later, we have absolutely no regrets about our ADU conversion project. The rental income has been a fantastic addition to our monthly budget, and we’ve had amazing tenants from the start. It has been the missing piece of our dream home and is making a more secure financial future possible for our family.

If you’re considering adding an ADU to your home or property, here are a few things to keep in mind:

While we had been happy in a two-family home, we mistakenly thought we could do better. But after moving into what was supposed to be our perfect, single-family home, we realized we had made a mistake. Our “dream” house began to feel like a financial burden that only sucked up money and never gave anything back. Staying put and adding a small apartment has given us so much more breathing room and transformed our forever home from a burden into a boon.

#7764. We Tested Ryobi’s $129 Pressure Washer — Here’s What It Can (and Can’t) Do

Can this portable power washer possibly compare to the real thing? We put it to the test.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Nothing sets you up for a better spring than taking some time for some seasonal cleaning in the fall, and one of the best tools for autumn home cleanup is a classic pressure washer. If you’ve got a surface or a screen you need sprayed, a pressure washer can deliver enough pressure for all kinds of scrubbing.

But even the most avid pressure washer advocates would tell you they’re also pretty cumbersome tools that require a lot of setup and garage storage space. That’s exactly why I wanted to try out this portable pressurized washer from Ryobi. The concept is intriguing, promising users a fraction of the size, cost and power of a standard pressure washer. I was very curious whether this tool would actually provide more cleaning power than a standard garden hose nozzle.

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Ryobi One Plus Electric Power Cleaner was how substantial the tool felt. I was expecting it to feel a little flimsy, but the tool felt well-built in my hands. It all assembled easily in just a few clicks, taking only a small fraction of the time it would’ve taken to set up a full-size pressure washer. And if you’re worried about water ruining your battery, don’t be. The entire battery chamber is enclosed by a tightly sealed plastic housing.

For this test, I decided to replicate a classic fall cleanup task: hosing down screens. I wanted a big surface to clean, so I pulled the screen door off the back door and set it up in the backyard. Then, I applied a light coating of flour to the middle of the screen and a light mist of water to lock the flour in place.

From there, I just had to finish setting up the Ryobi pressure washer. It comes with three different nozzles: two flat angled nozzles and one “turbo nozzle” that sprays the water in a speedy spiral. All I had to do was attach the pressure washer to a garden hose, and the tool was ready to go. Then I just set myself up in front of the screen with the pressure washer the recommended distance (1-2 feet) from the screen. ‘

All that was left to do was let it rip. The first thing that stands out when you use this portable pressure washer is that it feels a little underwhelming when you pull the trigger- especially if you’ve ever used a full-sized pressure washer. There’s not much kick, and the water leaves the nozzle at a steady but uninspiring speed. For a few seconds, I was worried the 700psi of pressure wouldn’t be enough to clean up the floury mess I’d created.

But my worries lessened the longer I used the tool. It was gentler than the pressure washers I’d used before, but it provided a consistent stream that quickly started knocking the flour loose from the screen. Things started going even better once I switched to the turbo nozzle. The spin action really helped compensate for the lack of PSI pressure. Within another minute, I had knocked off a ton of the sticky flour from the screen.

A post shared by Family Handyman (@familyhandyman)

So enough waffling… what’s the verdict? It’s pretty clear, as soon as you start using this tool, that the Ryobi tool isn’t going to fully replace a full-sized pressure washer… especially if you need to really blast something. But there are many use cases for a pressure washer where consistency is more important than power. And if you’ve ever accidentally damaged something with a pressure washer, the reduced power of this tool might even be something you consider a pro.

It took a while, but eventually the screen was sparkling clean- so clean, in fact, it was nearly invisible in the doorway. I should also point out that real-world conditions are rarely as messy as the sticky flour mess I created. If you just need to get dust off a screen or mud off a sidewalk, this tool is a significant upgrade over a simple stream from a garden hose. Ultimately, you’re trading power for portability, and whether that works for you will depend on the job you have to tackle. If it’s only needed for routine seasonal cleaning, this pressure washer could be perfect for you.

Just don’t expect it to peel paint off a pole.

#7763. 5 Spots for a Water Leak You Might Totally Miss—But Can Cost You

Published Oct 29, 2026 4:05 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plumbing lines run throughout the home and the yard, bringing in fresh water for you to bathe, wash, water, and drink. However, when there is an issue with one of these plumbing lines or the attached appliances and fixtures, what seems like a small leak can quickly become a major problem as the growing accumulation of water causes water damage, encourages mold growth, and slowly ruins existing plumbing connections.

According to the EPA, the average household’s leaks can account for more than 9,300 gallons of wasted water per year, while some homes have leaks that waste 50 gallons or more per day. As a plumber and restoration expert, I have seen many issues that were easy enough to fix turn into major restoration projects simply because they were unseen or neglected for so long.

Even a single leak can destroy insulation, ruin drywall, and cause mold to spread behind your walls. Before your plumbing becomes a problem, use this guide to discover five water leak sources you might miss so that they don’t cost you in the long run.

Since this is a battery-powered unit, you don’t have to worry about missing a leak just because the power is out. Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Water-carrying appliance hoses, like those on refrigerators, dishwashers, and washing machines, are notorious for causing catastrophic, hidden water damage. Since these appliances are often pushed tight against walls or tucked inside cabinetry, a slow leak can be difficult to find as it quietly rots the subfloor for months before a puddle ever creeps out into the open room.

The wax ring or plastic flange connecting the toilet base to the waste pipe can degrade over years. Instead of leaking onto the bathroom floor, the water can seep straight down through the subfloor, rotting the ceiling framing of the room directly underneath, which is why you need to be aware of any potential signs of a water leak, especially in the bathroom.

Water leaks caused by frozen pipes hidden behind walls or under concrete slabs can go unnoticed for a long time, causing extensive water damage in the walls if you aren’t careful. Water lines running beneath a concrete slab foundation can corrode or shift, causing a slow leak. These are highly hidden and usually only identified by a warm spot on the floor, a spike in the water bill, or eventual foundation cracking.

Underground irrigation lines are one of the most common culprits behind massive, hidden water loss. Because irrigation systems are buried across a wide outdoor area, an underground leak can dump thousands of gallons directly into the soil without ever creating a surface puddle.

Like roof leaks, outdoor spigots can lead to unexpected damage over a long period of time. These spigots should be turned off during the winter to prevent them from bursting internally during winter freezes. However, they may also develop leaks during the warmer months of the year, and the leak can remain completely hidden inside the wall cavity or crawlspace, only letting water escape whenever the valve is opened.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

#7762. A Stylish Indoor Herb Garden With Nearly Zero Effort: An Auk Mini 2 Review

Published Oct 30, 2026 8:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I was already a fan of the original Auk Mini after testing it for our guide to the best grow lights, so I was curious whether the new Auk Mini 2 actually improved on it or simply gave it a facelift. I tested the Espresso/Walnut model on the same kitchen counter where I used the original: an area that receives virtually no natural light. That meant the plants were entirely dependent on the Mini 2’s built-in grow light. I planted all four included pots with the supplied seeds, two basil and two parsley, and grew them for about a month.

The biggest change I noticed right away was the design. The original Auk Mini was already one of the best-looking growing systems I’d tested, but the Mini 2 feels more finished. Its corners are rounder, the transitions between components are smoother, and the whole thing has a more organic shape. I tested the Espresso/Walnut finish again, and it’s still my favorite. The pots have changed, too. Their bottoms are more rounded and extend farther into the reservoir, which appears to give the growing medium better access to water.

Setup is still wonderfully simple. Auk gives you exactly enough prehydrated coco coir for the four pots, and I’ve yet to use another coco coir product that’s as pleasant to work with straight out of the bag. I filled the pots, planted the supplied basil and parsley seeds, scattered the included (and new) small stones over the growing medium, added water and nutrients, and installed the light. That was basically it. The new top layer might seem like a minor addition, but germination and early growth seemed noticeably quicker than with my original Mini. Auk claims the Mini 2 produces 20 percent more growth, and while I didn’t conduct a controlled comparison, my experience certainly supports the idea that plants establish faster in this version.

After roughly a month, all four plants had grown into full, healthy herbs that I was able to harvest for cooking. That’s particularly impressive considering they received no sunlight whatsoever. I didn’t encounter algae, mold, or other growing problems during testing. Maintenance was minimal, too. During the first month as the plants were establishing, I didn’t need to refill the water reservoir.

Once the herbs became established and started drinking more, I simply topped off the reservoir as necessary. At that point, trimming the herbs to keep their growth under control actually became more work than maintaining the garden itself, and that’s hardly a complaint when the payoff is fresh basil and parsley whenever I want them.

There are other upgrades, including an optional app, a new Slow Mode, a larger reservoir, and optional pots designed for larger plants. Those additions make the Mini 2 more versatile, but I don’t think existing Auk Mini owners need to rush out and replace their current unit. The original is still really well made. My biggest complaint is that at $249, I wish Auk included the two larger pots and longer dowels rather than charging another $79 for them. Still, for someone buying their first Auk, I’d absolutely choose the Auk Mini 2. It’s super easy to use, grows plants effectively with minimal effort, and actually looks good while doing it.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.
