#7717. How to Test Your Home’s Water Quality

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:05 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

We use water every day for drinking, cooking, cleaning, and bathing, but how often do we stop to think about what’s actually in it? Water that looks clean can contain potentially harmful contaminants, including lead, bacteria, and chemicals. The good news is, learning how to test water quality at home is pretty straightforward, whether you’re using an inexpensive DIY test kit, or you mail a sample to a certified laboratory. We’ll walk you through the testing process, explain what your results mean, and help you figure out what to do if you find a problem.

Even if your water looks clean doesn’t always mean it’s safe to drink. Contaminants and certain bacteria can be in there without changing the water’s appearance, taste, or smell. Testing your water helps identify potential health risks and gives you a clearer picture of what’s coming out of your faucets.

“A common misconception is that water is safe if it looks, smells and tastes fine,” says Dr. Eric Roy, Chief of Science at Culligan International. “But the reality is that contaminants such as lead, arsenic, and ‘forever chemicals’ (PFAS) cannot be detected by our senses.”

Water testing can also reveal less serious issues, such as high mineral content. Hard water, which contains elevated levels of calcium and magnesium, can cause scale buildup in pipes and appliances, leave spots on dishes, and make soap less effective. Testing can also help you get to the bottom of unpleasant tastes, unusual odors, or discoloration.

Knowing what’s in your water helps you decide whether you need a filtration system, a water softener, or another treatment method. And even if your water is perfectly safe to drink, you might still want to improve its taste or overall quality.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Testing your water quality is a simple process that takes just a few minutes of hands-on work, depending on the type of test you choose. At-home water test kits give you quick results for common water-quality indicators, while mail-in laboratory tests offer more detailed information about potentially harmful contaminants.

Before getting started, read the instructions included with your test kit carefully. Different tests have different sampling requirements, and even small mistakes, such as touching the inside of a collection bottle or flushing the faucet when you shouldn’t, can affect the accuracy of your results.

The best testing method depends on what you’re looking for. Inexpensive, at-home test kits typically use strips or color-changing solutions to check for pH, chlorine, and hardness. They’re useful for identifying common water-quality issues, but generally lack the precision to detect harmful contaminants at very low concentrations.

For health-related concerns, such as lead, arsenic, bacteria, or PFAS, choose a mail-in kit analyzed by a certified laboratory. As Dr. Jess Goddard, chief science officer at SimpleLab Inc. explains, “If you’re making a health decision or about to spend money on treatment, you definitely want lab results behind it.”

Safe Home’s mail-in water test kit checks 200 qparameters, including 7 inorganics, 31 metals, and 20 pesticides and herbicides. Read the review.

Before collecting your water sample, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water and clear the area around the faucet. Wipe away any visible dirt or debris, and remove the faucet aerator if your testing instructions require it. Some tests, particularly those for bacteria, may also require disinfecting the faucet opening before sampling.

Be careful not to introduce contaminants during preparation. Avoid touching the inside of collection bottles or their caps, and wear disposable gloves if recommended by your test kit. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as preparation requirements can vary depending on the contaminants being tested.

For many water tests, you’ll need to run cold water through the faucet for a couple of minutes before collecting your sample. This flushes out stagnant water that’s been sitting in your plumbing, helping you collect a sample representative of your incoming water supply. However, always check your kit’s instructions first, as some tests require a different approach.

“For example, some lead-testing protocols require collecting the first water from a cold tap after several hours without use,” explains Rich Razgaitis, co-founder and CEO of FloWater. “If you flush the pipes beforehand, you may wash away the very evidence you’re looking for.”

Once the faucet is prepared, collect your sample according to your test kit’s instructions. The process differs slightly depending on your testing method:

Keep your fingers away from bottle openings and inside surfaces to prevent contamination. Seal samples immediately and follow any storage or shipping instructions.

Now it’s time to test your sample. The process will depend on whether you’re using an at-home kit or sending your water to a laboratory.

Note: At-home kits aren’t always dip strips. Some use reagents, test vials, or incubation procedures for bacteria. Always follow the instructions for the specific kit you have.

Once you’ve tested your water, the next step is figuring out what the results mean. Most at-home testing kits use color-coded charts to indicate the concentration of different substances in your water, while laboratory reports provide more precise measurements, often in parts per million (ppm), parts per billion (ppb), or milligrams per liter (mg/L).

Compare your results with the reference ranges provided by the kit or laboratory, paying particular attention to any contaminants that exceed health-based guidelines. Keep in mind that detecting a substance doesn’t automatically mean your water is unsafe.

“When interpreting results, a common mistake is assuming that a detection automatically means you have a health risk,” explains Goddard. “You need to put the result in context, first, and compare the detected concentration to a health guideline to determine if there’s a problem.”

Here’s what some common water-quality findings mean and how to address them.

Water hardness measures the concentration of dissolved minerals, primarily calcium and magnesium. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, water containing 121 to 180 ppm of hardness (measured as calcium carbonate) is considered hard, while anything above 180 ppm is very hard.

Hard water is generally safe to drink, but it can cause mineral buildup in pipes, faucets, and appliances. If your results indicate hard or very hard water and you’re experiencing these problems, consider installing a water softener. These systems reduce calcium and magnesium levels to help prevent scale buildup.

iSpring’s water softener is an electronic magnetic softener that treats mineral buildup but doesn’t remove heavy metals from water. Read the review.

Lead can enter drinking water through old pipes, solder, and plumbing fixtures, particularly in older homes. There is no known safe level of lead exposure, so any detected lead deserves attention, especially in households with children.

If a lab test detects lead, use a verified safe drinking-water source while investigating the problem. Contact your water utility or local health department for guidance, and consider having your plumbing inspected. A water filter independently certified for lead reduction can help reduce exposure, but replacing lead-containing plumbing may be necessary to address the source.

Finding E. coli in drinking water is a serious concern because it indicates fecal contamination. If your test detects E. coli, stop drinking the untreated water and contact your local health department or water utility.

For private wells, a professional may recommend inspecting and disinfecting the well, followed by additional testing to confirm the water is safe. UV treatment or other disinfection systems may also be appropriate for certain ongoing bacterial problems.

Boiling water can kill many disease-causing microorganisms, but it won’t remove chemical contaminants such as lead or nitrates. Follow the specific guidance provided by your health department rather than assuming boiling will solve every water-quality problem.

Nitrates can enter groundwater through fertilizers, septic systems, and agricultural runoff. Elevated levels are particularly dangerous for infants because they can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.

The EPA’s drinking-water limit for nitrate is 10 mg/L measured as nitrogen (NO3-N). If your results exceed this level, switch to a verified safe water source for drinking, cooking, and preparing baby formula, and consult your local health department.

A reverse osmosis system certified for nitrate reduction may be an appropriate long-term solution. Do not boil nitrate-contaminated water, as evaporation can increase the nitrate concentration.

Arsenic and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can be present in drinking water without any noticeable change in taste, smell, or appearance. Both can pose health risks, depending on the substance and concentration.

If lab testing identifies levels above applicable health-based guidelines, use a verified safe drinking-water source while seeking advice from your health department or a qualified water-treatment professional.

Depending on the contaminant, an appropriately certified reverse osmosis or activated carbon filtration system may help. Check that the specific system has been tested and certified to reduce the substance identified in your results.

The Waterdrop G3P600 installs under the sink and has a digital display that monitors the presence of TDS in the water. Read the review.

Not every unusual result indicates a health risk. Elevated iron can cause reddish-brown staining, while chlorine may give treated municipal water an unpleasant taste or odor. High mineral concentrations can also affect how water tastes.

If testing confirms that the issue is aesthetic rather than a health concern, you may be able to address it with a relatively simple treatment system. Activated carbon filters can improve chlorine taste and odor, while specialized iron filters can help reduce staining caused by elevated iron levels.

“A filter that improves taste isn’t necessarily removing lead,” says Razgaitis. “A water softener addresses hardness, not every health concern. UV treatment targets microorganisms but doesn’t remove dissolved chemicals.”

Whatever your results show, choose a treatment system that is independently certified to address the specific contaminants in your water, rather than assuming any filter will do the job.

Testing your home’s water quality is a simple but important step toward making sure the water you use every day is safe. Whether you use an at-home testing kit or send a sample to a certified laboratory, following the proper collection instructions will help you get reliable results.

Remember: Not every unusual reading indicates a health risk, but potentially harmful contaminants should always be taken seriously. Once you understand what’s in your water, you can make informed decisions about whether filtration, water softening, or other treatment is necessary.

Yes, you can test your home’s water quality using an at-home testing kit. Most kits use test strips or chemical reagents to check for common water-quality indicators such as pH, chlorine, and hardness. However, DIY kits have limitations, particularly when detecting potentially harmful contaminants at very low concentrations. For more comprehensive testing, the EPA recommends using a state-certified drinking water laboratory.

Common signs of poor water quality include unusual tastes or odors, cloudy or discolored water, and staining around sinks and faucets. White, chalky residue on fixtures can also indicate hard water. However, these symptoms don’t necessarily mean your water is unsafe. According to the CDC, harmful germs and chemicals may be present without affecting how water looks, tastes, or smells.

At-home water tests are a convenient, inexpensive way to screen for basic water-quality issues, such as hardness, pH, and chlorine levels. However, laboratory testing is generally the better option if you’re concerned about contaminants such as lead, arsenic, PFAS, or bacteria. These tests require greater accuracy and sensitivity than most DIY kits can provide. For example, the CDC recommends using a state-certified laboratory to test private well water.

There’s no single list of five indicators that covers every drinking-water concern, but homeowners should pay particular attention to total coliform bacteria, nitrates, pH, total dissolved solids (TDS), and lead.

#7716. Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

What’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

Under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

“Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” says international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”

But RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

The biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

Over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:

Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he says. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”

A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”

“The biggest thing for me is convenience,” says environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”

Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he says.

Personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:

“Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” says Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”

If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

“Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” says Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”

For Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he says. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”

Otherwise, Daily says that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

If you’re currently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

Otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

#7713. Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

At some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

On the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

Set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

Drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

Insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

Thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

Connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

The strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

#7711. Want Year-Round Curb Appeal, Even in Winter? Try These 20 Stunning Plants

By Jennifer Noonan, Updated by Teresa Odle

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Does your home’s landscape look barren and brown after autumn leaves fall, and doesn’t perk back up again until spring? Most homeowners think about how their beds will look when they’re in full bloom, but few imagine how that same bed will look in the dead of winter. Outdoor winter plants that add beautiful contrast to a snowy landscape aren’t just good for your curb appeal—they can also provide critical food sources and nesting sites for wildlife. As you consider updates to the plants and shrubs that surround your home, look to these appealing, year-round options.

Blue Ice bog rosemary’s unique silvery-blue foliage looks good in every season, plus this evergreen ground cover delights with a shock of pink bell-shaped blooms in early spring. Perfect for rock gardens and moist soils, it will attract birds and bring visual interest to the yard all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 6Size: 1 to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Blue Ice Bog Rosemary at The Tree Center for $39.50

This dwarf pine variety turns from green to gold when cold weather arrives. In fact, the colder the climate, the more intense its color becomes. This rabbit- and deer-resistant plant is easy to care for, and an evergreen shrub that will look beautiful all year long. It grows slowly, but immediately adds low-growing color and texture to a winter bed.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: nearly 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Carstens Wintergold Mugo Pine at Mike’s Plants on Etsy for $75

Many weeping ornamentals lose their leaves in cold weather, but not the weeping Norway spruce. With its unusual shape and showy cones, this evergreen makes a great accent in the garden and provides rich green in all four seasons. It can thrive in many soil types, including rich sandy soils, and has low water needs once established.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 4 feet high and 15 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 3- to 4-foot high Weeping Norway Spruce at Spring Hill Nurseries for $299

This evergreen succulent creates a lush and attractive carpet that thrives year-round in cool to warm climates. Most boast tiny flowers that attract butterflies in summer, and the foliage of Pink Form and Purple Form can take on reddish to purple hues in colder months. Easy to care for in full sun, this little wonder packs a lot of life in its compact height but excellent spread. After a season or two, it is xeric.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: 1 feet high and 1 to 1.5 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 4-inch pot of Sedum Hispanicum at Cristina’s Garden on Etsy for $10.99

For evergreen ground cover in warmer climates, try Pot Belly Pittosporum. The tough little shrub flowers in spring and summer, leaving its silvery green foliage with a white underside on the plant through winter.  Best of all, it keeps its rounded shape with little maintenance required. Pot Belly Pittosporum is drought tolerant once established and can grow in partial to full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 8 to 11Size: 4 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Pot Belly Pittosporum at Cornell Farm for $28.99

This ground-hugging variety of dianthus is evergreen and cold hardy. Its gray-green foliage erupts in summer with flowers, making it a wonderful filler both in the garden and in pots, so feel free to grow it in a container and overwinter it indoors in colder zones. The flowers are also fragrant, adding a clove-like scent to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: about 1 foot high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Frosty Fire Dianthus at Holly Days for $11.99

If you’re looking for a distinctive shade of evergreen color, dwarf globe blue spruce delivers. This slow-growing, densely branched conifer has blue needles that become more brilliant in summer. It makes a wonderful low hedge, or stands out as a small rabbit-resistant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 2 to 3 feet high and 3 to 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Dwarf Globe Blue Spruce tree at Trees.com for $54.95

Pink pussytoe plants provide an evergreen mat of tiny silver-gray leaves. In late spring, the plant spikes deep pink, fuzzy flowers. It’s a slow grower and requires little water once established, so this cold-hardy beauty is a breeze to care for in any season. The native cultivar grows best in full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 0.5 feet high and 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 20 Pussytoes seeds at SeedCult on Etsy for $2.99

Snowdrop bulbs are happiest with cold or moderate winters, and are among favorite winter-flowering plants. Place them in full or partial where you can enjoy their delicate white flowers in the fall and throughout the cold months, even during snow. Come spring, they’ll go dormant.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: 0.5 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 25 Galanthus Nivalis bulbs at White Flower Farm for $20

Christmas rose, a variety of hellebore, is a pest-resistant evergreen perennial. It also provides valuable nectar for early pollinators, like the rusty patched bumblebee, who are seeking blooms in late winter or early spring. Find it a shady location with space to grow, and soon you’ll enjoy its white winter blooms in the warmer end of their growing range or early spring where colder.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 1 foot tall and up to 1.5 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Ivory Prince Christmas Rose at Plant Addicts for $49.99

Winter jasmine is a vining shrub that will treat you with bursts of fragrant yellow flowers between late winter and early spring; the plant’s flowers often are the first to appear as winter wraps up. But even when not in bloom, this plant’s large arching stems will provide plenty of visual interest to the garden. Hardy and easy to grow, winter jasmine is just at home in coastal areas as it is along rock walls.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 10Size: up to 10 feet tall and 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon pot of Winter Jasmine at The Home Depot for $25.58

Known for its medicinal properties, witch hazel is often used in cosmetics and lotions, since it is reported to reduce inflammation and soothe certain skin irritations. It’s also a great choice for a winter garden, thanks to its fragrant yellow-to-red flowers that can bloom even in snowy weather. This adaptable shrub or small tree thrives in full sun to partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 3 to 6 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1- to 2-foot high Witch Hazel at TN Nursery for $26.99

Named for its small clusters of white berries that put on a show throughout the winter and give way to little white flowers in the spring, the snowberry plant provides a valuable food source for birds during the cold winter months. This easy-care plant will spread as a dense thicket, so it’s a great choice for borders and living fences.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: more than 15 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted White Snowberry at The Home Depot for $38.04

Featuring dark green glossy leaves, sweet box plants are shade-loving evergreen shrubs that boast small fragrant flowers that bloom in late winter and early spring. Once the fragrant flowers fade, little black fruits will appear in their wake. Preferring partial to full shade, sweet box plants are tough and excellent year-round plants to add interest to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Fragrant Dwarf Sweet Box at Planting Partners on Etsy for $28.99

For a vibrant splash of color in warmer zones, plant winter heath in your yard, which will repay you with abundant tiny pink winter flowers that bloom in late winter through early spring. The colorful winter shrub is an even hardier version of E. carnea, and both are commonly used as a ground cover, forming a dense mat. Prune it right after it finishes flowering in the spring to prevent leafless stems and keep it looking great all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a quart-size potted Erica Kramer’s Red Winter Heath at The Home Depot for $18.53

This deciduous shrub’s large size creates a show-stopping garden accent. In mid- to late fall, the American cranberry bush will burst with vibrant red berries that last into winter. The berries  are edible but aren’t very tasty when eaten raw. However, they provide important winter food for wildlife. Fragrant while flowers appear in spring and persist through mid summer. The shrub thrives in full or partial sun and prefers alkaline soil.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: 8 to 12 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Bailey Compact American Cranberry Bush at Plant Addicts for $73.99

Also known as Perovskia, Russian sage is popular for its tall blue-violet flowers that bloom in the summer through the fall, attracting all sorts of pollinators to the garden. However, this shrub looks great in the winter, too, thanks to long silvery stems that offer structure and intrigue to a winter landscape. Leave the faded flower stems on until new growth appears in spring and plant Russian sage along walkways to maximize enjoyment of its fragrant flowers in summer. Once established, it is a drought-tolerant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: up to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-inch potted Lacey Blue Russian Sage at American Meadows for $7.99

Also known as Eastern teaberry, American wintergreen features glossy evergreen leaves and bright red berries that will offer a beautiful contrast to a wintery white landscape. Like many winter outdoor plants, this shrub helps small mammals and birds who love the berries. It is disease-resistant, and crushing its leaves will release a refreshing wintergreen scent. Plant the showy low grower in dappled sunlight to deep shade to keep it happy.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: less than 1 foot high and up to 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get 6 bare root Teaberry Wintergreen plants at New Hampshire Plants on Etsy for $9.99

Yucca glauca is among the most winter-hardy yucca varieties. Its attractive evergreen foliage features long narrow stems in a rosette shape that look great all year long. In the spring, a stem rises from the rosette that features white bell-shaped flowers. These flowers attract butterflies, and the entire easy-care yucca plant provides food and nesting opportunities for small mammals, birds, and reptiles.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 3 to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 5-inch pot of Soapweed Yucca at Etsy for $24.75

This low-growing shrub features glossy dark green leaves that turn bronze in the fall, persisting through the winter. During the winter you’ll also be treated to the shrub’s remaining vivid red berries, which provide a valuable food source for birds. The berries arise from tiny white flowers that form in the spring and summer, which butterflies love. Plant it in full sun to watch it thrive, though the shrub can handle partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 8Size: 1 foot high and 4 to 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Bearberry Cotoneaster Coral Beauty at Plants Express for $17.95

#7709. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”

#7708. This is Our Top Pick When Choosing an Air Filter for Your Home’s Furnace or AC

Updated Nov 3, 2026 8:25 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Air filters for furnace and home AC are designed to trap dust, dirt, bacteria, and other small particles. Depending on the MERV rating of the house air filter (which measures how well a filter removes particles), it may even be able to trap viruses and other microscopic debris. By removing contaminants from the air, the furnace filtration system improves indoor air quality and protects the internal components of the furnace and AC from the pollutants the return duct takes in.

Furnace and air conditioner filter replacement is essential for the ongoing health of the HVAC system. Our top choice is the Simply Filters 14x25x1 MERV 11 Air Filter, which is designed to trap dust, mold, pet dander, pollen, and even auto exhaust. Additionally, this replaceable air filter has a pleated and electrostatic construction for trapping contaminants, and it works with most furnace and AC brands. Use this guide to learn more about air filter replacement and discover our selection of the best air filters for furnace and home AC.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air filter enhances indoor air quality and HVAC efficiency. Consider MERV ratings, filter types, and proper sizing for optimal results.

Available in a range of sizes, this pack of six disposable air filters by Simply Filters is our top choice. Each air filter has a pleated and electrostatic design that attracts and traps dust and debris as small as 1 micron. The MERV 11 rating indicates that the air filter is effective against pollen, dust mites, mold, dust, pet dander, auto exhaust, and small allergens, though it does not filter ultrafine particles such as tobacco smoke, bacteria, or viruses.

The high pleat count improves capture coverage while optimizing airflow and air filtration efficiency for up to 3 months before the filter needs to be replaced. When it’s time to replace the air filter, refer to the airflow arrows on the filter frame to ensure it’s installed correctly. For best results, it’s recommended to use this air filter in conjunction with an air purifier or other allergen-reducing measures.

Get the Simply Filters air filters for furnace and home AC at Amazon or Walmart.

Choose one of the best furnace and AC air filters for home use from the products listed below to protect the HVAC system and improve indoor air quality.

Furnace and air conditioner filters are integral to the ongoing operation of the HVAC system, so it’s important to find out what you might not know about HVAC air filters. Learning more about air filters for furnace filtration can help you determine what to look for when choosing a furnace filter’s replacement, including the type of air filter and MERV rating, as well as furnace and air conditioner filter sizes.

Before picking up the first air filter you find, it’s a good idea to determine which type of air filter is best for the home and existing HVAC system. Even the best HVAC brands typically offer a variety of air filter options to choose from, so it’s recommended to learn more about home air conditioner filters, including washable, disposable, fiberglass, pleated, electrostatic, and polyester air filters.

Even the best energy-efficient air conditioners will suffer if they are not equipped with an appropriate air filter. Deciding on the right air filter can be difficult, though, without understanding the terms used to measure the filtration quality and efficiency. MERV stands for minimum efficiency reporting value, which is a number assigned to a product based on its density and filtration capabilities.

Andrew Hulsebos, service director for Reiner Group, a heating and air conditioning company in northern New Jersey, says that the MERV rating system ranges from 1 to 20, and that higher numbers indicate a higher level of filtration. “For residential use, air filters are typically rated between MERV 5 to 13.” Higher-efficiency filters are mainly used in commercial settings or health facilities that are equipped with powerful HVAC systems that are capable of drawing the air through the dense filters.

Furnace and AC air filters are available in a wide range of sizes and thicknesses, so it’s necessary to check the HVAC system operating manual to determine the right size for your system. Generally, if the filter needs to be bent, jammed, or otherwise forced into position, it’s too big. Similarly, the air filter may be too small if it doesn’t come within an inch of all four corners of the air handler slot or frame.

The easiest way to determine the right size air filter for the home is to check the existing air filter. The measurements are usually listed on the frame of the filter, making it easy to find the size. Alternatively, you can measure the existing air filter with a tape measure, or even measure the air intake slot to find out the appropriate size air filter for the HVAC system.

Homeowners will want to stay on top of a range of maintenance tasks to keep the home functional and comfortable, but knowing exactly what needs to be done isn’t always obvious. Before purchasing replacement air filters for furnaces and home AC, it’s worth checking out the answers below to some of the most frequently asked questions about HVAC air filters.

Yes, furnaces and AC units generally use the same air filter. “They share the same air handler, where the filter is located, which means you don’t need to worry about buying separate filters for each system,” says Hulsebos.

Yes. The most common HVAC configuration for residential properties typically involves the furnace and air conditioner sharing the same air filter, so to properly maintain the air conditioner, the furnace filter will need to be replaced or washed when necessary. How often to replace an air filter depends on the number of people and pets, and the frequency with which the home is used. On average, though, you should replace the filter about every 3 months.

The number of air filters in a house tends to depend on the size of the home, including the square footage, number of floors, and the number of HVAC units. Generally, a single air filter is enough for most residential properties, though larger homes may have more than one HVAC unit, each requiring at least one air filter.

HEPA air filters are often considered high-quality products with excellent filtration capabilities. However, Hulsebos notes that “part of the reason that HEPA filters are so rarely used in HVAC systems is that they are extremely restrictive in terms of airflow.” HEPA filters can also be expensive, difficult to clean, and typically need to be replaced every 6 to 12 months.

Residential HVAC systems usually require a filter with a MERV rating between 5 and 13. Air filters with higher MERV ratings may be able to filter smaller particles, but they may put unnecessary stress on the HVAC system as the blower attempts to force the air through the dense filter. So while a higher MERV rating can be better, the air filter needs to be paired with a suitable HVAC system for optimal performance.

Generally, the maximum MERV rating for a residential furnace is 13, though commercial or health care facilities may have more powerful HVAC systems that can operate normally while using air filters up to MERV 20.

The most commonly used air filter in an HVAC system is a pleated air filter. This is because it has high filtration capabilities and a relatively low price. These air filters can generally be purchased online or from a local home improvement store, though some grocery stores may also carry pleated air filters.

#7707. The Best Salt Spreaders of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Salt spreaders don’t get the attention they deserve. Though freshly fallen snow has a beautiful way of blanketing neighborhoods in a peaceful ambiance, it’s not long before cold concrete can turn that snow into slippery ice. Enter salt spreaders, which are simple tools that make it much easier and quicker to apply deicing salt to driveways, walkways, and other outdoor areas.

Though I’m a firm believer in safety first, I also acknowledge that using too much salt to melt accumulated snow and ice can damage concrete, harm plants and animals, and contaminate water. Salt spreaders help mitigate this problem by maintaining even distribution and keeping salt confined to intended areas.

To determine which salt spreaders are worth their price, we researched dozens of popular spreaders before testing six top options on our driveway and walkways, as well as on our front steps and deck. Our favorite was the Scotts Elite Spreader for its even and easy application, convenience and control, and ability to accommodate both granular and rock salt. Read on to see our test results for this and the rest of the products we recommend before choosing one of the best salt spreaders for your property.

Bottom line: Salt spreaders are essential for safe, efficient deicing. The Scotts Elite Spreader stands out, but other models offer great alternatives for various needs.

Our Ratings: Assembly 5/5; Distribution 4.75/5; Durability 4.5/5; Value 5/5

With a dual-rotor design, the Scotts Elite walk-behind salt spreader has an impressive 80-pound capacity and 6-foot spread width for quick salt application to driveways, sidewalks, and decks. It comes mostly assembled, other than attaching its 10-inch never-flat tires and flipping up its ergonomic handle. In our tests, we found it stable and easy to maneuver, even when filled with all 35 pounds of ice melt we had on hand.

The Scotts Elite salt dispenser for snow and ice features dial settings from two to 15, meaning it works with everything from fine lawn fertilizers to chunky rock salt. Since we’re careful to avoid unnecessarily applying ice melt for environmental and economic reasons, we wish this model featured its EdgeGuard technology next to both rotors instead of just one. Still, so long as we planned which direction we went when working next to our lawn, we found the application to be even and relatively easy to control.

What our tester says: “If I could only choose one salt and fertilizer spreader, this would be it. It holds a ton of product, moves easily over uneven terrain, and makes quick work of large areas.” —Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Scotts Elite salt spreader at Tractor Supply Co., Ace Hardware, or The Home Depot.

While we were happy to melt ice and snow with the help of our top pick, we understand that it may not be right for everyone. The following five spreaders also passed our tests and might be better for those with differing capacity needs.

There are hundreds of salt spreaders on the market, so choosing just a few to test wasn’t easy. To make our decision, we researched various types of spreaders, including everything from salt spreaders for trucks to simple feed scoops. Once we selected six options, we put each through a series of tests, including assembly, using them with granular salt and rock salt, and evaluating any additional features. We rated each product according to a rubric and gave the highest overall scorer our award for the best salt spreader.

When choosing the right salt spreader, there are a few important factors to keep in mind. These include the size of the surfaces in need of salting, which type of spreader you prefer, and the quality of materials, among other things.

The snow salt spreaders we tested for home use are exclusively walk-behind and handheld models. However, larger commercial settings may require a truck salt spreader or a salt spreader for a tractor.

Many residential salt spreaders are designed as compact handheld units. Scoop-style models are sometimes fully open, and others have lids with various-size holes to accommodate both granular and rock salt while helping control the amount of product dispensed at once.

A slightly more complex handheld salt spreader may feature a hopper up top and a mechanism that opens to allow salt to project from the front of the spreader. Open-top hopper-style units are available in hand-crank or battery-powered versions with dials to allow various sizes of ice through. These types of handheld units generally work best with granular salt and may clog with rock-style products.

Walk-behind salt spreaders are more substantial than handheld units, incorporating larger hoppers as well as wheels, handles, and a range of additional features. They’re better suited to larger surfaces where users want to cover a decent amount of square footage quickly. On the flip side, their size makes them tricky to use in tight spots and on stairs.

Our top picks for walk-behind spreaders project salt in widths between 4 and 6 feet and feature at least one fin or deflector to help control spread width as desired. Most walk-behind spreaders have a wide range of opening settings to accommodate small materials like fertilizer, substantial pieces of rock salt, and everything in between.

While we only tested handheld and walk-behind spreaders in this guide, towable and hitch-mount salt spreaders are also available for larger properties or commercial use. Towable electric salt spreaders can help users avoid having to rely on snow removal services for the job, although they do require mounting to a truck, ATV, or lawn tractor.

Perhaps the biggest factor to consider when choosing the best salt spreader is the size of the area in need of treatment before or after a storm. Since handheld units often hold only 5 pounds of salt or less, they’re better for smaller spaces like stairs or detailed work alongside the edge of a driveway.

Walk-behind units are helpful for driveways, sidewalks, and decks since they allow quick application over larger areas and often incorporate fins or deflectors to help increase accuracy. The walk-behind units we tested have a capacity of 80 to 130 pounds, though smaller and larger models are available. In our perfect world, we would own both a walk-behind and a handheld spreader for speed and precision.

Towable salt spreaders can hold over 100 pounds of salt, making them ideal for deicing sizable surfaces quickly. Generally speaking, though, they aren’t as accurate as smaller units.

Most salt spreaders are made with plastic hoppers since the material is lightweight, relatively durable, and easy to maintain. Steel or stainless steel salt spreaders may be more durable over the years, but they generally weigh more and will require additional maintenance to prevent rust.

Salt spreader handles and broadcast plates may also be made of either metal or plastic. As with the hopper, the use of metal in these parts may make them more durable but also heavier and in need of additional maintenance.

While the above sections cover the most important features of salt spreaders, you may still have a few questions if you’ve never used one. Below, we answer a few of the most common queries about these devices.

Salt spreaders are an efficient and affordable way to reduce the time and effort it takes to keep potentially slippery surfaces safe in winter. They can also help save on snow removal costs. We think they are worth it, especially if you live anywhere snowfall is a relatively common occurrence.

Many fertilizer spreaders work with salt, provided the salt is small and granular. If the opening is big enough, your current fertilizer spreader may even accommodate rock salt. If you don’t have a salt spreader but need to melt ice, our guide on how to melt ice without salt provides a few additional methods.

Yes, the best time to spread salt is before it snows. Salting an hour or more before a snowfall helps prevent snow from sticking. If you miss your window to salt before a storm, be sure to use a snow shovel to clear as much accumulation as possible before applying salt using a spreader.

There are two reasons why it’s far from ideal to leave salt in a salt spreader. First, salt is corrosive and can damage your spreader over time. Second, if moisture from the air or wayward rain or snow gets into your spreader and combines with the salt, you may end up with a frozen block of ice inside your machine.

Having spent half her life in the Midwest and the rest in the mountains, Michelle Larson is no stranger to snow or the amount of time it takes to remove it. Because she’d rather spend a little more upfront than buy a tool or appliance twice, she strongly believes in the power of product testing for finding quality items that are meant to last.

Check out our favorite products on sale during Prime Day! We found markdowns on power tools, garden accessories, robot vacuums, power stations, and more.

Michelle is a lifelong learner who lives and plays in the mountains of Park City, Utah, with her husband, daughter, and pets. She came to the Commerce team at BobVila.com in February 2022 with more than 5 years’ experience as a business owner, writer, and program manager.

#7706. Supreme Court to Consider Successive Habeas Claim in Capital Case, Twenty Years After the Murder

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

This week, the Court will consider when a death-row inmate may file a second habeas application based on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.”

On Wednesday this week, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in Guerrero, Director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice v. Dexter Johnson. It is a capital case involving the kidnapping, rape, and murder of Maria Aparece that Johnson committed in 2006. The case does not involve any claim Johnson is innocent of these heinous crimes, but rather how to interpret provisions in the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA).

AEDPA prohibits successive habeas applications by state prisoners with only two narrow exceptions, including for claims that "rel[y] on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A). The question presented seems to answer itself. The Supreme Court has granted cert to decide whether a claim relies on a "new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable" when the Court announced the rule before the filing of the prisoner's prior federal habeas petition. As Texas persuasively argues in its merits brief, Johnson's Atkins claim (that he should not be executed because, he claims, he is borderline intellectually disabled) does not rely on any new rule of constitutional law. The Court decided Atkins v. Virginia in 2002—long before Johnson filed his initial federal habeas application, before his conviction became final on direct review—and even before he committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.

Instead of a change in law, Johnson's claim relies on a new factual predicate: the publication of a new diagnostic manual by the American Psychiatric Association (the DSM-5), under which he was diagnosed with an intellectual disability. But a claim in a successive application based on a new factual predicate must satisfy § 2244(b)(2)(B), which Johnson's Atkins claim does not, because his new evidence has no bearing on whether the jury would have found him "guilty of the underlying offense." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii).

Surprisingly, a Fifth Circuit panel accepted Johnson's argument that he could pursue relief on this "new" claim. And the Fifth Circuit en banc denied further review by a vote of 9-7. Judge Ho (joined by Judges Jones, Smith, and Engelhardt) wrote a dissent from this denial, pointing out that "[e]xtraordinary delays like this are, alas, extraordinarily commonplace in our criminal justice system. And they are far from costless. Never mind the expense to the taxpayer. Such delays also force the family and friends of victims like Maria Aparece to wait for justice—for over two decades, in this case."

I have filed an amicus brief in the case, along with counsel of record Allyson Ho and her colleagues at Gibson Dunn, Brad Hubbard, Matt Scorcio, Brandon Wolf, and Marquan Robertson. Our brief provides a fuller account of the cost to victims' families—such as the Aparece family—who must wait for justice in capital cases like this one. Here's the introduction to our brief:

Twenty years ago, in the early-morning hours of Father's Day 2006, Dexter Johnson abducted 23-year-old Maria Chrisalee Lopez Aparece—"Sally" to her family and friends—and her boyfriend, Huy Ngo, at gunpoint. After terrorizing them, Johnson raped Sally in the back seat of her car while his accomplice taunted Ngo. Johnson then marched Sally and Ngo into the woods, shot each of them in the head, and left them for dead. Johnson and his accomplices then took Sally's car joyriding and used her credit cards to fund a shopping spree. Earlier that evening, Sally had been at home making a card for her father, Protasio Aparece, while he worked a sixteen-hour shift as a registered nurse. After her murder, Sally's family found the unfinished card. They placed it in their living room, in front of the fireplace, alongside Sally's ashes—where it remains today. Johnson's vicious crimes inflicted unbearable pain on his victims and their families.

But that was just the beginning of their suffering. Johnson's serial litigation has robbed the families of even a modicum of peace or closure. It has been two decades since Johnson brutally murdered Sally, and nineteen years since a Harris County jury sentenced him to death—but justice still has not been served. This Court should vindicate crime victims' "important interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence," Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149 (2019), and "powerful and legitimate interest" in "real finality," Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998), by reversing the judgment below and ending an ordeal that has compounded the suffering of Sally's family for over two decades.

You can read the full brief for the Aparece family here, which discusses how excessive delays (like the one in this case) break AEDPA's promise of finality in capital cases and how research confirms that excessive delays in criminal cases harm victims' families.

I hope the Court reverses the Fifth Circuit's decision and brings the Aparece family one step closer to justice.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 2, 2010

Paul Cassell is the Ronald N. Boyce Presidential Professor of Criminal Law and University Distinguished Professor of Law at S.J. Quinney College of Law at the University of Utah.

#7705. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.
